s1.title: A Stock Is a Slice of Ownership
s1.p1: Imagine you and two friends open a coffee shop with $300,000 of combined capital. You divide ownership into 300,000 equal slices worth $1 each. You put in $90,000, so you own 90,000 slices — 30% of the business. A stock is simply the certificate for those slices.
s1.p2: To raise money, a company can split ownership into millions or even billions of slices and sell them to the public. Each slice is one share. Buyers become shareholders: they are not lending money to the company, they genuinely own a small piece of it.

key.title: Key idea
key.text: A stock represents a share of ownership in a company. It is not a loan, not a deposit, and it promises no fixed return.

s1.f1: 1 share = one small slice of company ownership
s1.f1note: Your percentage of shares determines how much of the company you own.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A company has issued 1,000,000 shares in total.
example.l2: If you own 1,000 shares, you own 1,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.1% of the company.

myth.title: Common myth
myth.text: “Buying stock means lending money to the company, which must pay me back.” That describes a bond. Stocks represent ownership; the company does not promise to repay you.

pro.title: Professional definition
pro.text: An equity security represents a residual claim on a company. After all debts are paid, shareholders share the remaining assets and profits in proportion to their ownership.

s2.title: Shareholders, Public Companies and Limited Liability
s2.p1: A public company is one whose shares can be bought and sold on a public exchange. Any eligible investor can buy its shares and become one of its owners.
s2.p2: As a shareholder you have several basic rights: to vote in proportion to your shares at the annual meeting; to receive dividends in proportion to your shares when they are paid; to share in any remaining value after a liquidation pays off debts; and to sell your shares to someone else at any time.

list.title: Four basic shareholder rights
list.i1: Voting: vote on major company matters in proportion to your shares
list.i2: Dividends: receive payouts in proportion to your shares
list.i3: Residual claim: share in what remains after a liquidation pays creditors
list.i4: Transfer: sell your shares to other investors

pro.title: Limited liability
pro.text: Shareholders can lose at most what they invested. Company debts are not pursued against personal assets (except in cases such as fraud). This limited liability is one reason stock investing became widespread.

myth.title: Common myth
myth.text: “If the company loses money, shareholders must pay extra.” Normally they do not. Limited liability protects personal assets.

tip.title: About this game
tip.text: Every company, price, financial statement and news item in this game is fictional. It exists for education and must not be used for real investment decisions.

s3.title: Exchanges and Tickers
s3.p1: An exchange is an organised marketplace where buyers and sellers post quotes, get matched and trade. The exchange itself does not buy or sell shares; it provides rules, systems and oversight.
s3.p2: Every listed company has a ticker symbol, such as AURA or VRDN in this game. It works like the stock's ID in the market. Real tickers are usually one to five letters.

list.title: What exchanges do
list.i1: Match buy and sell orders
list.i2: Publish trade prices and volume
list.i3: Set listing, disclosure and trading rules
list.i4: Maintain market integrity and investor protection

example.title: Examples in this game
example.l1: AURA is the ticker for Auralis Robotics.
example.l2: VRDN is the ticker for Verdant Foods. Tickers let you find a company quickly.

warn.title: Keep in mind
warn.text: A company can list on several exchanges with different tickers. A ticker is only an identifier; it says nothing about whether the company is a good investment.

s4.title: Share Price vs Market Capitalisation
s4.p1: The share price is the current market price of one share. It updates constantly as buyers and sellers trade: when someone is willing to pay more, the price rises.
s4.p2: Market capitalisation is the total market value of the whole company: share price × shares outstanding. A high share price does not mean a big company — market cap reflects overall size.

key.title: The difference
key.text: Share price tells you what one share costs. Market cap tells you what the whole company is worth.

s4.f1: Market cap = share price × shares outstanding
s4.f1note: Shares outstanding = every share the company has issued.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: AURA trades at $42.50 and has 180 million shares outstanding.

warn.title: Common myth
warn.text: A low share price does not mean a company is cheap. A $5 stock can be more expensive than a $500 stock once you consider market cap, earnings and share count.

tip.title: Try it
tip.text: Open any company in the Market and watch its market cap change with the share price. Inspecting two companies completes Unit 1's practice task.

s1.title: How a Buy or Sell Happens
s1.p1: You place an order through a broker. The broker sends it to an exchange, where the trading system matches it. When a buyer and seller agree on a price, the trade executes.
s1.p2: Buying means you gain shares and pay cash. Selling means you give up shares and receive cash. When the price rises, the same shares sell for more; when it falls, for less.

list.title: Five steps of a trade
list.i1: Choose the stock and quantity
list.i2: Choose the order type (market or limit)
list.i3: Submit the order
list.i5: Your cash and positions update after the fill

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: You buy 20 shares at $50 with $1,000 and pay a $1 commission.
example.l2: Your position grows by 20 shares and your cash falls by $1,001. The money did not vanish; it changed from cash into stock.

myth.title: Common myth
myth.text: “The money disappears after I buy.” It becomes stock. Apart from the fee, total assets simply change form.

s2.title: Cash, Positions and Total Equity
s2.p1: A trading account holds two things: cash and positions. Cash is buying power you can use immediately. A position is the quantity of shares you own and what they cost.
s2.p2: When you buy, cash falls and the position grows. When you sell, the position shrinks and cash rises. Ignoring fees, total equity is unchanged at the moment of the trade.

key.title: Remember this identity
key.text: Total equity = cash + the market value of all positions. Price changes move total equity, not cash.

s2.f1: Total equity = cash + Σ (shares × current price)

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Start with $10,000 cash, then buy $5,000 of stock and pay a $1 commission.
example.l2: Cash becomes $4,999, the position is worth $5,000, and total equity is about $9,999.

warn.title: Keep in mind
warn.text: Fees reduce total equity slightly. That is a real cost of trading, not a system error.

s3.title: Market Orders and Execution Price
s3.p1: A market order asks to trade immediately at the best price currently available. It prioritises speed of execution, not a specific price.
s3.p2: The “last price” you see is the price of the previous trade, not necessarily your next fill. Buys usually execute at the ask; sells usually execute at the bid.

list.title: Three traits of market orders
list.i1: Fast execution
list.i2: No price guarantee
list.i3: Slippage is possible when liquidity is thin or volatility is high

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: The last price is $50.00, with a bid of $49.98 and an ask of $50.02.
example.l2: A market buy of 10 shares fills at $50.02, not $50.00. The difference is the spread cost.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: With volatile or thinly traded stocks, a market order can fill far from the price you saw. That is slippage.

s4.title: Bid, Ask and the Spread
s4.p1: The bid is the highest price a buyer will currently pay. The ask is the lowest price a seller will currently accept. The gap between them is the spread.
s4.p2: The spread is an implicit trading cost: buy and immediately sell, and you usually lose a little to the spread. More liquid, actively traded stocks usually have tighter spreads.
s4.f1: Spread = ask − bid; spread cost ≈ spread × quantity

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Bid $49.98, ask $50.02, so the spread is $0.04.
example.l2: Buy 100 shares and sell immediately and the spread alone costs about $4 (before commission).

tip.title: Try it
tip.text: Check the bid and ask in the quote strip on the Trading page, and compare them before and after you place an order.

s1.title: Cost Basis and Market Value
s1.p1: Cost basis is the total amount you paid for a position, including the purchase price and the buy commission. Average cost = cost basis ÷ shares held.
s1.p2: Market value = current price × shares held. The difference between the two is your unrealized profit or loss.
s1.f1: Unrealized P&L = current market value − cost basis

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Buy 20 shares at $50 with a $1 fee: cost basis is $1,001 and average cost is $50.05.
example.l2: If the price is now $55, market value is $1,100.

warn.title: Keep in mind
warn.text: Including the buy fee in cost basis makes it clearer what price you actually need to break even.

s2.title: Realized vs Unrealized P&L
s2.p1: Unrealized P&L is the gain or loss while you still hold the shares; it moves with the price. Realized P&L is locked in once you sell.
s2.p2: While you hold, the P&L is only a book number. Selling converts it into cash. Realized gains add cash; realized losses reduce it.

key.title: One-line summary
key.text: You only realize it when you sell. Paper gains can vanish; realized P&L is final.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Buy at $50; at $60 the unrealized gain is $10 per share.
example.l2: If the price falls back to $52, the unrealized gain is only $2.
example.l3: Sell there and the realized P&L is that $2 (before fees).

s3.title: Return on Investment
s3.p1: Return expresses P&L as a percentage of the capital invested: return = P&L ÷ cost × 100%.
s3.p2: Returns let you compare trades of different sizes: $100 profit is 10% on $1,000 of capital, but only 0.1% on $100,000.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Cost basis $1,001; net sale proceeds $1,099.

tip.title: Going further
tip.text: Annualised return converts returns over different holding periods into a one-year equivalent. Later stages cover this in detail.

s4.title: How Fees Change Your P&L
s4.p1: A commission is a service fee charged by a broker or platform. It can be a flat amount per order or a percentage of the traded value.
s4.p2: Fees come out of your cash and directly reduce gains or deepen losses. Trading frequently turns fees into a significant drag — one reason overtrading is a problem.
s4.f1: Net profit = sale proceeds − purchase cost − buy fees − sell fees

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Buy $1,000 of stock with a $1 commission, then sell for $1,100 with another $1 commission.
example.l2: Net profit is $98, not $100.

warn.title: Keep in mind
warn.text: This game charges a flat $1.00 virtual commission per fill. Real-world fee structures are more complex and may include commissions, regulatory fees, spreads and taxes.

s1.title: Trading Sessions and Market State
s1.p1: Real markets have fixed sessions (for example, US equities trade 09:30–16:00 Eastern Time) and are closed on weekends and holidays. Nothing executes while the market is closed.
s1.p2: This game uses a simulated clock: each trading day has eight time steps. You can pause, run at 1× / 5× / 20×, or fast-forward to the next session. Orders only match while the market is running.

list.title: What the clock can do
list.i1: Pause or resume the simulated market
list.i2: Switch between 1×, 5× and 20× speed
list.i3: Fast-forward to the next trading day
list.i4: See the current trading day and session time

warn.title: Real-market note
warn.text: Pre-market and after-hours trading have lower liquidity, wider spreads and higher risk. This game simplifies by not simulating extended hours.

s2.title: Market Orders: Pros and Costs
s2.p1: A market order is the simplest instruction: fill immediately at the best available price. It suits situations where execution matters more than price.
s2.p2: The trade-off is price uncertainty. You control quantity and direction, not the fill price.

list.title: Market orders
list.i1: Pro: high likelihood of execution and speed
list.i2: Risk: no price lock
list.i3: Risk: slippage in volatile conditions
list.i4: Use case: liquid stocks and situations that need immediate execution

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: You see $50.00, but the price jumps to $50.40 as you submit.
example.l2: Your market order fills at $50.40, costing an extra $0.40 per share.

s3.title: Limit Orders
s3.p1: A limit order sets the maximum price you will pay (buy) or the minimum you will accept (sell). It only fills at that price or better.
s3.p2: Buy limits sit below the market, waiting for a pullback; sell limits sit above the market, waiting for a rally. Limit orders guarantee price, not execution.
s3.f1: Buy limit: fill ≤ limit; sell limit: fill ≥ limit

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: With the market at $50, you place a buy limit for 100 shares at $48.
example.l2: It only fills if the ask drops to $48 or lower. If the stock keeps rising, the order may never fill.

list.title: Two behaviours for buy limits
list.i1: Limit below the market: rests in the order book waiting for a pullback
list.i2: Limit above the market: may fill immediately at a better prevailing price

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Limit orders can miss opportunities: if the price never returns to your level, you stay in cash while the stock rallies.

s4.title: Fills, Resting Orders and Liquidity
s4.p1: Orders have states: open, filled, cancelled and rejected. An unfilled limit order rests in the order book until it fills or you cancel it.
s4.p2: Liquidity describes how easily a stock trades and how close fills are to the expected price. Active stocks have good liquidity, tight spreads and less price impact from size.
s4.p3: Large orders can sweep several price levels and cause market impact, worsening the average fill. This game simplifies execution to the top of book, but spreads and slippage still exist.

table.r1c2: Submitted and waiting for the price condition
table.r2c2: Executed; cash and positions have updated
table.r4c2: Not enough cash or shares, so the order could not stand

tip.title: Try it
tip.text: Check your open orders on the Trading page and cancel them if needed. Limit orders match automatically as the simulated price moves.

s1.title: Cash dividends: sharing profits with shareholders
s1.p1: When a company earns money it can reinvest it in the business or pay part of the cash out to shareholders. The latter is a dividend, also called a cash distribution.
s1.p2: A dividend is not free money: on the ex-dividend date the share price usually adjusts down by roughly the dividend per share. You receive cash while the market value of your holding falls, so total value is broadly unchanged at that instant.
s1.f1: Cash dividend = shares held × dividend per share
s1.f1note: This game pays quarterly: dividend per share = starting price × annual yield ÷ 4.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: You hold 100 shares and the dividend is $0.60 per share, so you receive $60 in cash.
example.l2: The price was $40.00 before the ex-date and adjusts to about $39.40, reducing the position value by about $60.

key.title: Key idea
key.text: Dividends come from company profits and cash flow. They are not guaranteed: a company can cut, suspend or cancel them.

myth.title: Common myth
myth.text: "A higher yield is always better" is false. A high yield can come from a falling share price or from a one-off payout that cannot last.

s2.title: Dividend yield: putting the payout next to the price
s2.p1: Dividend yield links the dividend per share to the share price. It tells you what percentage of cash income you would receive in a year at the current price.
s2.p2: When the price falls, the same dividend per share produces a higher yield. That does not mean the company became more generous; the shares became cheaper, which may also signal rising risk.
s2.f1: Dividend yield = annual dividend per share ÷ current price × 100%
s2.f1note: Yield moves with the share price; the dividend per share is usually declared quarterly.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Annual dividend per share is $1.20 and the price is $40.00, so the yield is 1.20 ÷ 40 = 3.00%.
example.l2: If the price falls to $30.00 the yield becomes 4.00%, but the company still pays $1.20 per share.

list.title: Why the yield changes
list.i1: The company raises or cuts the dividend per share
list.i2: The share price rises or falls
list.i3: One-off special dividends and cyclical industry profits

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Dividend yield is not a fixed interest rate. The company may cut the payout and the price may keep falling; both affect your real return.

s3.title: The ex-dividend date: cash in exchange for price
s3.p1: After declaring a dividend the company sets a record date and an ex-dividend date. In the standard convention, holders before the ex-date receive the payment; buyers on or after the ex-date do not.
s3.p2: This game simplifies the process: at the close of the ex-date it credits cash to your account and adjusts the share price down by roughly the dividend amount. You see cash rise and position value fall.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: You hold 200 shares and the dividend is $0.50 per share, so you receive $100 on the ex-date.
example.l2: The price moves from $25.00 to about $24.50, leaving total value broadly unchanged at that instant.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Taxes, trading costs and price moves around the ex-date mean receiving a dividend is not the same as gaining that amount. This game does not model dividend taxes.

tip.title: Try it
tip.text: Use the demo below to change shares, price and yield, then watch annual cash flow and the ten-year reinvestment result.

s4.title: Dividend reinvestment and total return
s4.p1: Total return has two parts: price change (price return) and dividends (income return). Looking only at the share price ignores cash payouts.
s4.p2: Reinvesting dividends buys more shares, which increases the base for future dividends and compounds over time, but the result still depends on the share price.
s4.f1: Payout ratio = dividend per share ÷ earnings per share; total return ≈ price return + dividend return
s4.f1note: A higher payout ratio leaves less profit inside the company for reinvestment.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: EPS is $2.00 and the annual dividend is $1.00, so the payout ratio is 50%.
example.l2: Half of earnings goes to shareholders; the other half stays in the business for growth or debt reduction.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Sustainable dividends usually come from stable free cash flow. A high payout ratio can limit reinvestment or force a cut when earnings fall.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Dividend reinvestment is not risk-free compounding: prices can fall and payouts can be cut. A historical yield is not a promise.

s1.title: Growth stocks: paying for growth
s1.p1: Growth stocks grow revenue and earnings faster than the market average. They usually reinvest most profits into research, expansion or acquisitions, so dividends are small or zero.
s1.p2: The market pays a higher valuation for sustained growth. If growth slows or expectations miss, both the valuation and the share price can fall, so growth stocks are often more volatile.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Two companies both earn $1 per share. The market pays 40× earnings for the growth stock, about $40, and 15× for the mature company, about $15.
example.l2: The extra you pay for the growth stock buys future growth expectations, not current earnings.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: High valuations must be justified by sustained growth. If growth disappoints, the share price can fall sharply.

s2.title: Value and cyclical stocks
s2.p1: Value stocks trade low relative to earnings, assets or cash flow. They may be undervalued, or cheap because fundamentals are deteriorating; cheap alone is not a reason to buy.
s2.p2: Cyclical stocks have profits that swing with the economy, common in industrials, materials, energy and discretionary consumer sectors. Earnings can be strong in expansions and fall quickly in recessions.

list.title: What to check when judging style
list.i1: Revenue and earnings growth
list.i2: Valuation such as P/E and P/B
list.i3: Dividend yield, industry cycle and earnings stability

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Style labels are not permanent. Companies grow, mature or decline; classification is a starting point, not a substitute for fundamental research.

s3.title: Income stocks and judging style
s3.p1: Income companies are usually mature with stable cash flow, distributing a larger share of profits as dividends, but with limited growth.
s3.p2: Do not rely on the label alone. A high yield can come from a falling price; a growth stock may start paying dividends; a cyclical stock can look cheap at a cycle peak.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A $50 share paying $2 a year yields 4%.
example.l2: If the price falls to $25 while the dividend stays $2, the yield becomes 8%, but the market may be worried about a cut.

myth.title: Common myth
myth.text: "Value stocks are always safe and growth stocks always make money" are both false. Style describes characteristics, not guaranteed returns.

tip.title: Try it
tip.text: Open companies with different styles in the market, compare their sectors, yields and valuations, then decide which risk you are willing to take.

s1.title: ETFs: one ticker, a basket of assets
s1.p1: An ETF is a basket of assets traded on an exchange, with a ticker and a quote like a stock. It usually tracks an index, sector or theme.
s1.p2: Buying one ETF share gives indirect exposure to all its components, so it is diversified by construction. Costs are usually below active funds, but management fees and spreads still apply.

list.title: Common ETF types
list.i1: Broad index ETFs covering the whole market
list.i2: Sector and thematic ETFs concentrated in one area
list.i3: Bond, commodity and other asset ETFs

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Diversification is not the absence of risk. Sector ETFs can be highly concentrated, and broad ETFs still fall with the overall market. Completing Unit 7 unlocks five tradable ETFs with live quotes that can be bought, sold and shorted like stocks.

s2.title: Diversification and correlation
s2.p1: Diversification spreads money across different assets to reduce company- or sector-specific risk. It cannot remove overall market risk.
s2.p2: The benefit depends on correlation: assets that always move together provide little diversification, while low-correlation assets usually produce a smoother portfolio.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A single stock has 30% annualised volatility; spreading money equally across three companies in different sectors may produce lower portfolio volatility.
example.l2: If all three are in the same sector and fall together, the diversification benefit is much smaller.

s3.title: Building your own basket and rebalancing
s3.p1: You can build your own ETF with 3–5 stocks from different sectors, bought at target weights.
s3.p2: Prices move and weights drift. Rebalancing sells what has grown and buys what has shrunk to restore the target weights and control risk.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Target one third each with $9,000 total, so $3,000 per stock.
example.l2: If one position grows to $4,000, rebalancing sells about $333 and adds it to the other two.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Rebalancing costs commissions and can reduce short-term returns; its main purpose is controlling risk exposure, not guaranteeing a higher return.

tip.title: Try it
tip.text: In the practice task, buy at least three stocks from different sectors to experience diversification.

s1.title: Simple versus compound interest
s1.p1: Simple interest is paid only on the original principal. Compound interest adds each period's interest to the principal so that future interest is earned on it too.
s1.p2: Compounding depends on time and reinvestment. With the same annual return, starting earlier produces faster growth later.
s1.f1note: This assumes annual compounding and a constant return with all interest reinvested.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: $1,000 at 8% compounded annually for 10 years: 1000 × 1.08^10 ≈ $2,158.92.
example.l2: The same conditions for 20 years: 1000 × 1.08^20 ≈ $4,660.96. Doubling time more than doubles the result.

s2.title: Regular contributions and the power of time
s2.p1: Regular contributions amplify compounding because every new deposit also earns future returns.
s2.p2: Compounding is very sensitive to return. 7% versus 10% over 30 years is a huge difference, but higher assumed returns usually mean higher risk.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: $1,000 initial plus $100 a month at 7% for 20 years ends near $56,000.
example.l2: About $25,000 comes from contributions and the rest from compounding; change the demo parameters to verify.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Nominal returns must cover fees and inflation. Real purchasing power growth can be much lower than the headline number.

s3.title: Long-term investing, drawdowns and inflation
s3.p1: Long-term investing is not set-and-forget. You still need to control concentration, fees and risk, and revisit your assumptions.
s3.p2: Drawdowns are asymmetric: a 50% fall requires a 100% gain to recover, and a large drawdown significantly slows the compounding curve.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Historical returns do not guarantee future results. The compounding demo excludes taxes, inflation and price volatility.

tip.title: Try it
tip.text: In the practice task, hold one stock for at least 15 trading sessions and observe how time and volatility affect your return.

s1.title: The four prices inside a candle
s1.p1: A candlestick records the open, high, low and close for one period. This game uses daily candles, so each candle is one trading session.
s1.p2: The body spans open to close. The upper wick reaches the high and the lower wick reaches the low. A close above the open is a bullish (green) candle; a close below the open is bearish (red).

example.title: Worked example
example.l2: This is a bullish candle: body $3.20, full range $5.50, upper wick $0.80 and lower wick $1.50.

s2.title: Timeframes and volume
s2.p1: The same market looks different across timeframes. Daily candles show trend better, while short timeframes contain more noise. The trading page offers 45 and 90 sessions.
s2.p2: Volume bars show how actively the asset traded in that period. Rising price with rising volume is often more convincing, but heavy volume on a decline can also mean panic selling.

list.title: Reading order
list.i1: First the trend and location
list.i2: Then the body and the wicks
list.i3: Finally volume and fundamentals

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: One candle cannot predict the future. The same shape means something different in an uptrend, a downtrend or a range.

s3.title: Common shapes and mistakes
s3.p1: A long upper wick shows a rally that faded; a long lower wick shows a dip that recovered; a doji means open and close were close together.
s3.p2: Shapes are traces of supply and demand, not guaranteed signals. Read them together with trend, volume and news context.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A long upper wick at the end of an uptrend can signal stronger selling pressure.
example.l2: A long lower wick in a downtrend can show buying support, or simply a brief bounce.

tip.title: Try it
tip.text: Switch the trading page to the advanced layout to see 90 daily candles and volume, then change open, high, low and close in the demo to watch the body and wicks move.

s1.title: Moving averages: smoothing noise
s1.p1: SMA is the arithmetic average of the last N closes. It smooths short-term noise and helps show trend direction.
s1.p2: Price above a moving average is often described as short-term strength. SMA20 crossing above SMA50 is called a golden cross; the reverse is a death cross. Both are descriptions, not guarantees.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: The last three closes are $10, $11 and $12.

s2.title: RSI: momentum and overbought/oversold
s2.p1: RSI compares recent gains and losses on a 0–100 scale. The common thresholds are 70 and 30.
s2.p2: RSI above 70 means strong recent upward momentum; it may be overbought, or it may stay high in a strong trend. Below 30 is the mirror image.

list.title: Using RSI
list.i1: Overbought does not mean it must fall now
list.i2: Strong trends can stay at extremes for a long time
list.i3: Combine it with trend, volume and fundamentals

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Indicators are computed from past prices, lag by construction and cannot predict news or earnings shocks.

s3.title: Limits and combining indicators
s3.p1: Different parameters produce different signals. SMA20 plus SMA50 is steadier than a single average, but still lags.
s3.p2: Indicators help confirm trends, size positions and manage risk; they are not a hunt for a guaranteed signal.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: An uptrend with moving averages aligned and RSI in a neutral range is usually more reliable than RSI alone being overbought.
example.l2: If price breaks below SMA50 on rising volume, the trend may already be weakening.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Indicators describe, they do not forecast. Any backtest must avoid look-ahead bias and overfitting or the result is meaningless.

s1.title: The income statement: revenue to profit
s1.p1: The income statement starts with revenue, subtracts operating costs and expenses and ends with net income. Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue; net margin = net income ÷ revenue.
s1.p2: EPS = net income ÷ shares outstanding, the denominator of the P/E ratio. The quality of profit growth matters more than a single year.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Revenue $1,000M, gross profit $520M, net income $200M.
example.l2: Gross margin is 52% and net margin 20%; with 100M shares, EPS is $2.00.

s2.title: The balance sheet: where assets come from
s2.p1: The balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity at a point in time. Assets are what the company owns; liabilities and equity are how it is financed.
s2.p2: The accounting identity is assets = liabilities + equity. Too much debt raises interest costs and financial risk.
s2.f1note: This game's statements are generated from company fundamentals and keep the identity, but are simplified simulations.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: The statements in this game are simplified teaching simulations, not audited reports, and must not be used for real investment decisions.

s3.title: Cash flow and earnings quality
s3.p1: Net income is not cash. Free cash flow = operating cash flow − capital expenditure, and it funds dividends, buybacks and debt repayment.
s3.p2: Check whether profit is backed by cash, whether receivables or inventory are growing unusually, and whether debt is rising quickly.

list.title: Three checks
list.i1: Is revenue growth supported by cash flow?
list.i2: Are margins stable or improving?
list.i3: Can free cash flow cover dividends and interest?

tip.title: Try it
tip.text: Switch the trading page to the advanced layout and inspect two companies' simplified income statement, balance sheet and free cash flow.

s1.title: DCF: discounting future cash back to today
s1.p1: DCF discounts future free cash flow to today's value. The discount rate reflects time value and risk: higher risk means a higher rate and a lower valuation.
s1.p2: Terminal value usually uses a perpetual growth model. Enterprise value minus net debt gives equity value; divide by shares for value per share.
s1.f1: EV = Σ FCF_t ÷ (1+r)^t + TV ÷ (1+r)^n; TV = FCF_n × (1+g) ÷ (r − g)
s1.f1note: r is the discount rate, g the perpetual growth rate, and r must exceed g.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Simplified: next year's FCF is $100M, the discount rate is 10%, with no terminal value.
example.l2: Present value = 100 ÷ 1.10 ≈ $90.91M.

s2.title: Assumptions drive the result
s2.p1: Growth, discount rate and perpetual growth are extremely sensitive inputs. A small change in assumptions can double or halve value per share.
s2.p2: Terminal value often dominates enterprise value, so check that perpetual growth stays below long-run economic growth.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: DCF is a thinking framework, not a precise answer. Use scenarios (bull, base, bear) instead of a single point estimate.

s3.title: Margin of safety and model limits
s3.p1: Valuation gives a range, not an exact price. A margin of safety is the buffer between the purchase price and intrinsic value, absorbing assumption errors.
s3.p2: DCF can fail for cyclicals, loss-making companies and fast-changing industries. Cross-check with relative valuation and asset value.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: The DCF in this game is a simplified teaching model, not investment advice; real valuation needs fuller statements and assumptions.

tip.title: Try it
tip.text: Change growth and the discount rate in the demo, watch value per share move, then decide which assumption is least certain.

s1.title: Growth, inflation and interest rates
s1.p1: GDP measures an economy's output. Faster growth usually supports corporate earnings, but overheating can bring inflation and rate hikes.
s1.p2: The cycle moves through expansion, slowdown, recession and recovery. Industrials, materials and discretionary consumer stocks are more cyclical; staples and utilities are more defensive.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Growth 3%, inflation 2%, policy rate 2.5%.
example.l2: Real rate = 2.5% − 2% = 0.5%, a relatively loose environment for risk assets.

s2.title: Inflation and purchasing power
s2.p1: Inflation is a broad rise in prices and erodes the purchasing power of cash and fixed income. Moderate inflation often comes with growth; high inflation can force central banks to raise rates.
s2.p2: Companies with pricing power may pass costs through; cost-sensitive and highly indebted companies feel more pressure.

list.title: What to watch
list.i1: CPI and core inflation trends
list.i2: Wages and commodity prices
list.i3: Central-bank language and rate expectations

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Macro data is revised and lagged; one month does not define a trend. Do not treat a single print as a certain signal.

s3.title: How rates affect valuation
s3.p1: Higher rates raise the cost of capital and the discount rate, usually pressuring equity valuations. High-growth stocks are more sensitive to the discount rate.
s3.p2: Rate cuts do the opposite; rates also affect bond prices, currencies and corporate funding costs.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: With the same cash flows, the discount rate rises from 8% to 10%.
example.l2: The present value of long-dated cash flow can fall 15–20%, and the valuation contracts.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Rates connect macro and valuation. Use scenarios (hike / unchanged / cut) rather than betting on one path.

s1.title: Asset allocation sets the portfolio's character
s1.p1: Asset allocation determines the risk and return structure of a portfolio and matters more than any single stock pick. Stocks, bonds and cash have different expected returns and volatility.
s1.p2: Weights decide the profile: more stocks usually mean higher expected return and volatility; cash lowers volatility but also long-run return.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: 60% stocks (7% expected, 16% volatility) plus 40% bonds (3.5%, 6%).
example.l2: Weighted expected return is about 5.6% and weighted volatility about 12%; actual portfolio volatility can be lower with diversification.

s2.title: Correlation and the limits of diversification
s2.p1: Lower-correlation assets produce a smoother portfolio; when everything moves together, diversification helps little.
s2.p2: More holdings is not always better. Over-diversification adds management cost and dilutes conviction; what matters is whether the risks are genuinely different.

list.title: Checklist
list.i1: Sector and single-position concentration
list.i2: Cash weight and liquidity
list.i3: Regular rebalancing and risk budget

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Historical correlations change; in a crisis assets can fall together, and diversification cannot remove systematic risk.

s3.title: Rebalancing and discipline
s3.p1: Prices move weights away from target. Rebalancing sells what has grown, buys what has shrunk and restores the intended risk exposure.
s3.p2: Rebalancing too often raises costs; rebalancing too rarely lets risk drift.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Target 60% stocks / 40% bonds, but stocks rise to 70%.
example.l2: Sell about 10% of the portfolio from stocks and buy bonds to return to target.

tip.title: Try it
tip.text: Change stock and bond weights in the allocation demo, then inspect concentration, volatility and max drawdown in Portfolio.

s1.title: Position sizing: risk first, shares second
s1.p1: Define the risk you can accept per trade (for example 1% of the account), then use entry and stop prices to calculate shares.
s1.p2: Position size = risk amount ÷ risk per share. A wider stop means a smaller position; a tighter stop allows more shares.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Account $10,000 with 1% risk = $100; entry $40 and stop $36.
example.l2: Risk per share is $4, so the position is 100 ÷ 4 = 25 shares, worth $1,000.

s2.title: Drawdowns and concentration
s2.p1: Drawdown is the fall from a peak in equity. A 50% loss requires a 100% gain to recover.
s2.p2: A large single position magnifies drawdowns; concentration and correlation determine the portfolio's real risk.

list.title: Basic risk controls
list.i1: Set stops and accept gap risk
list.i2: Limit single-position and sector weights
list.i3: Hold cash and avoid excessive leverage

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Stops can be jumped by gaps and do not guarantee execution at the stop price. A stop is not the absence of risk.

s3.title: Risk budgeting and survival
s3.p1: A risk budget allocates total risk across positions and strategies. When correlation is high, add risk together instead of treating positions as independent.
s3.p2: The goal of risk management is to survive and preserve the ability to compound, not to win every trade.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Two highly correlated trades each risk 1%.
example.l2: Combined risk is closer to 2% than to a diversified 1%.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Control risk before chasing return. Limiting drawdowns usually matters more than maximising a single trade, because large losses break compounding.

s1.title: Four common strategies
s1.p1: Value buys undervalued assets, growth buys high growth, momentum follows trends and dividend strategies focus on cash returns.
s1.p2: Every strategy has environments where it works and periods where it fails; none works all the time.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Rising rates often pressure high-valuation growth stocks.
example.l2: In an economic recovery, cyclical and value styles may outperform.

s2.title: Momentum and trend
s2.p1: Momentum buys recent winners and sells recent losers, assuming trends persist.
s2.p2: In choppy markets momentum gets whipsawed; it needs cost, turnover and stop-loss discipline.

list.title: Momentum design
list.i1: Define the lookback and rebalance frequency
list.i2: Control turnover and trading costs
list.i3: Avoid look-ahead bias and validate out of sample

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Past momentum is not future momentum; a strong backtest can be overfitting or an in-sample illusion.

s3.title: Combining strategies with discipline
s3.p1: Strategies can be combined, but watch overlapping holdings and rising correlation.
s3.p2: Define entry, exit, sizing and risk with rules instead of trading on feelings.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Value plus dividend strategies are usually more defensive.
example.l2: Growth plus momentum is more aggressive in bull markets, with potentially larger drawdowns.

tip.title: Try it
tip.text: Switch the 30 / 60 / 90 session window in the strategy demo and compare the four styles; this is simulated history, not a promise.

s1.title: How short selling works
s1.p1: Short selling borrows shares and sells them, hoping to buy them back lower. You profit from the gap between the sale price and the repurchase price, not from company growth.
s1.p2: The flow: borrow from the broker, sell at market, buy back (cover) after a decline, then return the shares and pay borrowing costs. Until you cover, you owe those shares.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Short 100 shares at $50 and receive $5,000.
example.l2: Cover at $40 for $4,000, locking in $1,000 before costs.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Short losses have no theoretical ceiling because the price can rise far above your sale price. Insufficient margin triggers forced liquidation.

s2.title: Costs and collateral
s2.p1: Short proceeds are usually not free to spend; they serve as collateral. The broker also requires extra margin to cover the risk of a rising price.
s2.p2: Borrowing shares has a fee, and if the company pays a dividend the short seller owes it. A rising price erodes collateral and can trigger a margin call.

list.title: Main costs of a short
list.i1: Stock borrow fee
list.i2: Dividends owed
list.i3: Collateral lock-up and financing cost

info.title: Simplified in this game
info.text: The simulation requires 50% of the short market value as collateral. Dividends are deducted as a liability; the borrow fee is not charged separately yet.

s3.title: When to cover
s3.p1: You can cover voluntarily, or the broker can force a buy-in when margin runs short. Planning the stop and position size matters more than calling the exact top.
s3.p2: Shorting expresses an overvaluation view or hedges a long, but it is a poor long-term hold: borrow costs, dividends and squeeze risk keep accumulating.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Short $2,000 of stock; a 50% rally loses $1,000.
example.l2: If that position used only 50% collateral, account equity is hit hard.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Shorts usually pair with strict stops and event-driven research. In illiquid names, a short squeeze can make covering dramatically more expensive.

s1.title: Margin accounts and leverage
s1.p1: A margin account lets you borrow cash to buy more stock, and uses short proceeds as collateral. Leverage magnifies both gains and losses.
s1.p2: Initial margin sets how large a position you may open; maintenance margin is the minimum equity the account must retain.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: With $10,000 of your own cash, buy $15,000 of stock using a $5,000 loan: 1.5x leverage.
example.l2: A 10% price drop loses about $1,500 of equity, which is 15% of your own cash.

s2.title: Financing interest
s2.p1: The debit balance accrues interest daily, usually by converting an annual rate to each trading day. The longer you hold, the more interest accumulates.
s2.p2: Interest directly reduces cash and equity. Even with a flat price, a leveraged position slowly bleeds.
s2.formula: Daily interest = debit balance × annual rate ÷ 252
s2.note: This simulation uses an 8% annual rate and 252 trading days as a teaching assumption.

list.title: What drives financing cost
list.i1: Size of the debit balance
list.i2: Annual interest rate
list.i3: Holding period in days

s3.title: Maintenance and forced liquidation
s3.p1: When equity falls below the maintenance requirement the account gets a margin call. If it cannot be met, the broker forces positions to be sold.
s3.p2: Forced liquidation usually happens at an unfavourable price, turning paper losses into permanent ones. Higher leverage makes the trigger easier to hit.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: After a margin purchase, the stock falls 35%.
example.l2: Equity may fall below the maintenance requirement and all positions are liquidated.

warn.title: Leverage cuts both ways
warn.text: Leverage does not raise your win rate; it only amplifies outcomes. Start small to learn how interest and liquidation work.

s1.title: Stop orders
s1.p1: A stop order becomes a market order once the trigger price is reached. Sell stops protect longs; buy stops protect shorts.
s1.p2: Place the trigger where you genuinely accept that the thesis is wrong, not at an arbitrary level. The fill can differ from the trigger.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Buy at $100 and place a sell stop at $92.
example.l2: When the price falls through $92 the order triggers and fills at the prevailing bid.

s2.title: Trailing stops
s2.p1: A trailing stop tightens as the price moves favourably but never loosens. It combines letting profits run with locking in part of the gain.
s2.p2: The trail can be set as a dollar amount. Volatile stocks need a wider distance, otherwise normal noise knocks you out.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Buy at $100 with a $6 trail; at $120 the stop moves up to $114.
example.l2: A pullback triggers the exit but still locks in $14 before costs.

list.title: Before setting a trailing stop
list.i1: Check the volatility
list.i2: Avoid an overly tight distance
list.i3: Accept slippage after the trigger

s3.title: Execution, gaps and slippage
s3.p1: A stop order does not guarantee the stop price. On a gap down or with thin liquidity, the fill can be materially worse.
s3.p2: A stop-limit can cap the price but may not fill at all; a market stop guarantees an exit but not a price.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: In extreme conditions stops trigger together and slippage widens. Never treat a stop as risk-free insurance.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: The stop is at $50, but the next open gaps to $42.
example.l2: The market stop fills near $42, far below the trigger.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Use position size to absorb gap risk and stops to limit everyday drawdown; they cannot replace each other.

s1.title: The order book and the spread
s1.p1: The order book lists bids and asks by price. The gap between the best bid and the best ask is the spread.
s1.p2: The spread is the immediate cost of trading. Better liquidity usually means a tighter spread; small or obscure names trade wider.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Bid $49.99 and ask $50.01: the spread is $0.02.
example.l2: Buying 100 shares immediately costs about $2 in spread.

s2.title: Depth, liquidity and slippage
s2.p1: Depth is the quantity available at each price. A large order eats several levels, so the average fill moves away from the best quote: that is slippage.
s2.p2: Liquidity also depends on time, news and volatility. Around the open, the close and major events, depth can thin out quickly.

list.title: Signals to watch
list.i1: Bid-ask spread
list.i2: Size at each level
list.i3: Volume and volatility

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: This simulated book is derived from the quote for teaching. Real depth changes quickly and includes hidden orders.

s3.title: Large orders and market impact
s3.p1: Orders larger than visible depth push the price up (or down). Slicing orders, using limits and spreading execution over time reduce impact.
s3.p2: Limit orders protect price but may only fill partially; market orders prioritise completion and pay with slippage.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Buy 2,500 shares when the first two levels hold only 1,500.
example.l2: The remaining 1,000 keep lifting offers, so the average price sits above the best ask.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Evaluate both price and probability of completion. Large capital cares more about market impact than a single commission.

s1.title: The four contract terms
s1.p1: An option gives the buyer the right, not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying at the strike on expiry. The buyer pays a premium for that right.
s1.p2: A contract usually covers 100 shares; the expiry sets how long the right lasts. This game uses European options that can only be exercised at expiry.

list.title: Every option contract specifies
list.i1: Underlying asset
list.i2: Strike price
list.i3: Expiry date

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: AURA trades at $50; a 30-day $55 call costs $1.20.
example.l2: One contract costs $1.20 × 100 = $120 before commission.

s2.title: Calls and puts
s2.p1: A call gives the buyer the right to buy the underlying at the strike; a put gives the right to sell it at the strike.
s2.p2: Buyers pay the premium and have limited loss; sellers collect the premium but carry the obligation. This stage is long-only.

info.title: Scope of this game
info.text: Only buying is supported for now: hold to expiry or close early at the model value. Selling options and multi-leg strategies come later.

s3.title: Strike and premium
s3.p1: The strike determines intrinsic value: a call is worth max(spot − strike, 0); a put is the reverse.
s3.p2: Premium = intrinsic value + time value. Time value shrinks toward expiry and grows with volatility.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Spot $52 and a $50 call have $2 of intrinsic value.
example.l2: If the premium is $3.10, time value is $3.10 − $2 = $1.10.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: The premium can go to zero. The buyer’s maximum loss is the premium paid, but that does not raise the odds of winning.

s1.title: The logic of buying calls
s1.p1: A long call expresses a bullish view. A small premium controls 100 shares, so both gains and losses are amplified.
s1.p2: A rally magnifies the payoff; without a rally the premium can expire worthless. Time hurts buyers, volatility helps them.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A $50 strike call costs $2, so one contract costs $200.
example.l2: At expiry the stock is $60: intrinsic $10 × 100 = $1,000, a $800 profit.

s2.title: Payoff and breakeven
s2.p1: Expiry P&L = max(spot − strike, 0) × 100 × contracts − premium paid.
s2.p2: Breakeven = strike + premium per share. The stock must finish above that level for the buyer to profit.
s2.formula: Expiry P&L = max(S − K, 0) × 100 × contracts − premium
s2.note: S is the expiry price and K the strike; commissions and taxes are excluded.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A $50 strike call with a $2 premium breaks even at $52.

list.title: Check before buying a call
list.i1: How far the strike sits from spot
list.i2: Premium as a share of the account
list.i3: Whether a catalyst remains before expiry

s3.title: Time and volatility
s3.p1: Theta erodes the premium every day and accelerates near expiry. Even a correct direction can lose money if it takes too long.
s3.p2: A drop in implied volatility also lowers the premium, which can offset a rally in the underlying.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Buying a call is not a guaranteed bullish trade. The stock must rise enough, fast enough, to beat time decay.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Size positions to cap premium spend and treat options as limited-risk expressions, not a sure path to leverage.

s1.title: The logic of buying puts
s1.p1: A long put gives the right to sell at the strike, so its value rises when the underlying falls.
s1.p2: Puts can speculate on a decline or insure an existing holding; the premium is the insurance cost.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A $50 strike put costs $2, so one contract costs $200.
example.l2: At expiry the stock is $40: intrinsic $10 × 100 = $1,000, an $800 profit.

s2.title: Put payoff
s2.p1: Expiry P&L = max(strike − spot, 0) × 100 × contracts − premium paid.
s2.p2: Breakeven = strike − premium per share. The stock must finish below that level for the buyer to profit.
s2.formula: Expiry P&L = max(K − S, 0) × 100 × contracts − premium
s2.note: S is the expiry price and K the strike; commissions and taxes are excluded.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A $50 strike put with a $2 premium breaks even at $48.

list.title: Check before buying a put
list.i1: How far the stock must fall to profit
list.i2: Whether the premium is fair insurance
list.i3: Whether the expiry gives enough time

s3.title: Protective puts
s3.p1: Stock plus a long put is a protective put: downside is capped, at the cost of the premium.
s3.p2: Insurance is not free. Continuous protection drags on long-term returns, but it helps around uncertain events.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Hold $10,000 of stock and buy a $45 strike put for $200.
example.l2: If the stock crashes, the maximum loss is capped by the strike and the premium.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Compare insurance cost with the drawdown you can tolerate. Do not over-insure noise, but do not stay naked into major events either.

s1.title: Intrinsic and time value
s1.p1: Premium = intrinsic value + time value. Time value reflects the possibility of future moves.
s1.p2: Implied volatility is the market’s price for future movement. Higher volatility makes options more expensive.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Spot $52 and a $50 call have $2 of intrinsic value.
example.l2: At a $3.10 premium, time value is $1.10 and shrinks toward expiry.

s2.title: The five Black-Scholes inputs
s2.p1: The model prices European options from spot, strike, time to expiry, volatility and the risk-free rate.
s2.p2: Volatility and time matter most to buyers; rates have a smaller effect.
s2.formula: Call = S · N(d1) − K · e^(−rT) · N(d2)
s2.note: This game uses a 4% risk-free rate and simulated company volatility; results are teaching estimates only.

list.title: Five inputs
list.i1: Spot S
list.i2: Strike K
list.i3: Time to expiry T

s3.title: The Greeks
s3.p1: Delta measures how much the premium moves for a $1 move in the underlying; gamma measures how fast delta changes.
s3.p2: Theta is time decay, vega is volatility sensitivity and rho is rate sensitivity.

list.title: The five Greeks
list.i1: Delta: directional sensitivity
list.i2: Gamma: speed of change in delta
list.i3: Theta: daily time decay
list.i4: Vega: effect of a 1 point volatility move
list.i5: Rho: effect of a 1 point rate move

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Use Greeks to manage portfolio risk, not to predict direction. Watch delta and theta first, then volatility exposure.

s1.title: Selling options for premium
s1.p1: Selling an option collects premium immediately but transfers the obligation to the buyer. The buyer chooses whether to exercise.
s1.p2: A short call’s maximum profit is the premium while its loss can be far larger; a short put’s maximum loss is the strike minus premium.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Sell one $50 call for $2 and collect $200.
example.l2: At expiry the stock is $60: pay $10 × 100 = $1,000, a net loss of $800.

s2.title: Collateral and assignment
s2.p1: Short options need collateral: a cash-secured put reserves strike × 100 in cash, while uncovered calls need extra margin.
s2.p2: In-the-money short options are assigned at expiry. This game cash-settles intrinsic value; real brokers may deliver stock.

list.title: Check before selling
list.i1: Whether cash or shares cover the obligation
list.i2: The worst-case loss
list.i3: Whether you accept buying or delivering at the strike

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: A naked call has no theoretical loss limit. Do not confuse a high win rate with low risk.

s3.title: The seller’s time advantage
s3.p1: Time favours sellers: theta erodes option value every day, so the contract can be bought back cheaper.
s3.p2: Rising volatility, gaps and event risk can still expand losses quickly, so position size is critical.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Sell a $2 put; if the stock finishes flat the premium expires worthless.
example.l2: The gain is $200 before collateral costs, but a break below the strike changes the picture fast.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Selling is risk management, not prediction. Define the maximum loss first, then judge the return.

s1.title: Covered calls: rent out your shares
s1.p1: Hold 100 shares and sell one call to create a covered call: the stock covers delivery in exchange for premium.
s1.p2: A strong rally caps upside because the shares are called away; a decline is only partly cushioned by premium.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Hold 100 shares at $50 and sell a $55 call for $1.50.
example.l2: Below $55 you keep the shares and $150; above $55 the shares are delivered at $55.

s2.title: Cash-secured puts: willing to buy
s2.p1: Sell a put and reserve strike × 100 in cash: you collect premium in exchange for a possible purchase at the strike.
s2.p2: Below the strike you buy at the strike; above the strike the premium is yours.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Sell a $45 put for $1.20 and reserve $4,500 cash.
example.l2: Above $45 you keep $120; below $45 you buy at $45, an effective cost of $43.80.

list.title: When it fits
list.i1: You are happy to own the stock
list.i2: The strike is below your fair value estimate
list.i3: The cash is genuinely spare

s3.title: The trade-off in income strategies
s3.p1: Covered calls and CSPs raise the win rate and lower volatility, but give up upside or cash flexibility.
s3.p2: They work well in range-bound markets and can lag simple ownership in strong trends.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Premium is not free income. Assignment, missed upside and opportunity cost are real costs.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Treat income strategies as position management tools, not a promise of steady cash flow.

s1.title: Bull call spreads
s1.p1: Buy a lower-strike call and sell a higher-strike call: that is a bull call spread.
s1.p2: The short leg lowers the debit and caps upside. Maximum loss is the net debit; maximum profit is the strike width minus that debit.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Buy the $50 call for $3 and sell the $55 call for $1: net debit $2.
example.l2: Above $55 the maximum profit is ($55 − $50 − $2) × 100 = $300.

s2.title: Bear put spreads
s2.p1: Buy a higher-strike put and sell a lower-strike put: that is a bear put spread.
s2.p2: The short leg lowers cost and keeps risk defined while expressing a bearish view.
s2.formula: Maximum profit = (strike width − net debit) × 100 × contracts
s2.note: Both legs share an expiry and opposite sides; a positive net debit means you pay up front.

list.title: When building a spread
list.i1: Use the same expiry
list.i2: Make sure the net debit is affordable
list.i3: Check whether the capped profit justifies the risk

s3.title: Why use spreads
s3.p1: Spreads cut premium cost and define maximum loss, which suits traders with a directional view who do not want to pay for a single leg.
s3.p2: The trade-off is capped profit; a huge move can leave the spread far behind a naked option.

info.title: In this game
info.text: Strategy cards pick two legs with the same expiry and different strikes, then validate cash against the net debit.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: A spread is a risk-budget tool. Size from maximum loss first, then decide whether the capped return is enough.

s1.title: Long straddles
s1.p1: Buy a call and a put with the same strike and expiry: that is a long straddle, a bet on large movement rather than direction.
s1.p2: Maximum loss is the two premiums; either direction can profit, but the move must clear the breakevens.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A $50 straddle with a $2 call and a $2 put costs $400.
example.l2: Breakevens are $54 and $46, so the stock must move a long way.

s2.title: Long strangles
s2.p1: Buy an out-of-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put: that is a long strangle, cheaper but needing a larger move.
s2.p2: The breakeven range is wider, which suits big events where at-the-money premium is too expensive.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A $55 call for $1 and a $45 put for $1 cost $200.
example.l2: The stock must exceed $56 or fall below $44 to profit.

list.title: Before buying volatility
list.i1: Is the event big enough
list.i2: Is implied volatility already rich
list.i3: Could the market calm down before expiry

s3.title: The risk in volatility trades
s3.p1: Long volatility fights time decay and falling implied volatility; a flat market erodes both legs.
s3.p2: Buying when implied volatility is high means even a move can be offset by an IV collapse.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: A straddle is not “profit either way”. The buyer only wins if movement exceeds what the market already priced.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Compare implied with historical volatility before an event. Expensive volatility needs an extreme move to pay.

s1.title: Futures contracts and margin
s1.p1: A future is an agreement to buy or sell the underlying at a set price on a future date. Longs face rising prices; shorts face falling prices.
s1.p2: Each contract covers 100 shares. Opening requires roughly 15% margin, but P&L is calculated on the full notional.

list.title: Contract terms
list.i1: Underlying stock
list.i2: Expiry date
list.i3: Multiplier (100 shares)

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A $50 future has $5,000 notional and about $750 margin.
example.l2: At $55 the long gains $500, roughly 67% of the margin.

s2.title: Daily mark-to-market
s2.p1: Futures settle to the latest price every day: gains are credited to cash and losses are debited as variation margin.
s2.p2: Leverage means small price moves can change equity dramatically, and repeated losses can exhaust margin.
s2.formula: Daily variation = (settlement − prior settlement) × direction × contracts × 100
s2.note: Direction is +1 for longs and −1 for shorts; this game applies it at each day close.

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Futures are not free leverage. Losses can exceed the initial margin.

s3.title: Expiry, basis and cash settlement
s3.p1: Futures usually trade above spot (contango); the gap is the cost of carry and it converges toward expiry.
s3.p2: This game cash-settles at the spot price on expiry instead of delivering shares.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Spot $50 and a 60-day future at $50.33 give a $0.33 basis.
example.l2: At expiry the basis converges to zero and futures equal spot.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Futures suit hedging and directional trades, but margin, basis and roll costs belong in the risk budget.

s1.title: How hedging works
s1.p1: Hold stock and short an equivalent futures notional to offset a decline; the hedge swaps directional risk for basis and margin risk.
s1.p2: The hedge ratio sets how much notional to short: 1.0 is a full hedge, 0.5 hedges half.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Hold 1,000 shares at $50 for $50,000.
example.l2: Short 10 $50 futures with $50,000 notional for a full hedge.

s2.title: Basis and correlation risk
s2.p1: Hedges are imperfect: basis changes, dividends, liquidity and correlation all leave residual risk.
s2.p2: Hedging a single stock with an index future introduces cross-hedge error.

list.title: Sources of residual risk
list.i1: Basis changes
list.i2: Falling correlation with the index
list.i3: Margin and liquidity pressure

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: A hedge lowers directional risk but never removes all risk. Correlations can jump in a crisis.

s3.title: Portfolio hedging in practice
s3.p1: Measure portfolio notional, short futures by the hedge ratio, and rebalance so the hedge does not drift.
s3.p2: Hedge costs include margin, basis and fees; compare them with the drawdown you want to avoid.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A $50,000 portfolio with a 60% hedge target.
example.l2: Short $30,000 notional, or six $50 contracts.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Hedging is part of the risk budget. Decide how much directional exposure to keep, then pick the tool.

s1.title: Leverage and liquidity spirals
s1.p1: High leverage lets losses erode equity quickly, forcing sales; sales push prices lower and trigger more liquidation.
s1.p2: Liquidity thins under stress, spreads widen and both slippage and margin requirements rise.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: $10,000 equity at 3x leverage with a 20% decline.
example.l2: The loss is about $6,000; equity falls to $4,000 while exposure stays large.

s2.title: Contagion and correlation
s2.p1: In a crisis correlations converge toward one, so a diversified portfolio falls together.
s2.p2: Counterparty, funding and collateral chains turn local losses into systemic risk.

list.title: Crisis signals
list.i1: Spreads and volatility spike
list.i2: Margin requirements rise
list.i3: Correlations jump

warn.title: Risk note
warn.text: Historical correlation does not guarantee future diversification. Stress-test for synchronized declines.

s3.title: Stress testing and survival
s3.p1: Ask what happens to the account in a −20%, −35% or −50% scenario, not just the average return.
s3.p2: Cash buffers, lower leverage and avoiding concentration are what carry an account through a crisis.

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: $20,000 equity, 2x leverage, a 30% decline.
example.l2: The loss is about $12,000, leaving $8,000; at 4x the account nearly wipes out.

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Survive first, optimise later. Keep worst-case losses inside what you can tolerate.

s1.title: Reviewing a multi-asset book
s1.p1: Stocks, options and futures carry different risks: direction, time value, volatility and margin.
s1.p2: The final challenge puts all three tools inside one risk budget instead of trading each in isolation.

list.title: Graduation checks
list.i1: A real stock trade
list.i2: A real option trade
list.i3: A real futures trade

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A $50,000 account with 1% risk and a $4 stop.
example.l2: Position size = $500 ÷ $4 = 125 shares instead of an arbitrary full position.

s2.title: Trading plans and risk budgets
s2.p1: Write the plan first: thesis, tools, maximum loss, exit conditions and review cadence.
s2.p2: Add up each trade’s worst case and keep the total inside the account’s tolerable drawdown.
s2.formula: Shares = account × risk% ÷ risk per share
s2.note: Risk per share = entry − stop; futures and options need margin or premium equivalents.

list.title: Plan template
list.i1: Thesis and invalidation
list.i2: Tools and sizing
list.i3: Maximum loss and review points

s3.title: The graduation task
s3.p1: Complete at least one real stock, option and futures trade while keeping the account alive.
s3.p2: The point is not short-term profit but whether you can explain each trade’s risk, cost and exit.

list.title: Self-check before submitting
list.i1: Every trade has an exit or stop
list.i2: Leverage and margin are tolerable
list.i3: You can explain the source of P&L in review

pro.title: Professional view
pro.text: Graduation is not about making the most money; it is about a repeatable, explainable process that controls risk.

s1.title: Fund NAV, subscriptions and redemptions
s1.p1: NAV = (market value of assets − liabilities) / fund shares. It measures what one fund share is worth, not how large the fund is.
s1.p2: Subscriptions add shares and assets; redemptions remove both. Market moves change asset value, so NAV changes when the share count is unchanged.

list.title: Three checks
list.i1: Valuation frequency: mark to market at each close
list.i2: Dealing price: usually today’s or next-day NAV
list.i3: Liquidity buffer: hold cash or liquid assets for redemptions

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Assets 120m, liabilities 10m and 10m shares give NAV = (120 − 10) / 10 = 11.
example.l2: If assets rise 10% with unchanged liabilities, NAV becomes 12.1. A 1m-share subscription raises AUM but leaves NAV broadly unchanged.

key.title: The key distinction
key.text: Return comes from asset performance, not from a larger AUM; growth in size is not investment return.

s2.title: Risk budgeting and rebalancing
s2.p1: A risk budget allocates total portfolio risk across assets or strategies. It looks at each position’s contribution to volatility, not only at capital weights.
s2.p2: Rebalancing pulls weights back to their target range, systematically selling what has risen and buying what has fallen to control concentration.

list.title: Three tools
list.i1: Volatility target: keep portfolio risk inside the budget
list.i2: Weight bands: allow small drifts and avoid pointless trades
list.i3: Cash and liquidity buffer: room for redemptions and opportunities

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A 60/40 portfolio drifts to 70% stocks; rebalancing sells stocks and buys bonds.
example.l2: With ±5% bands, weights between 55% and 65% can be left alone, reducing turnover cost.

key.title: The trade-off
key.text: Rebalancing reduces concentration risk but can give up trend returns and create trading costs; more frequent rebalancing costs more.

s3.title: Attribution, fees and redemptions
s3.p1: Performance attribution splits return into allocation, selection, interaction and fee drag, answering where the return came from.
s3.p2: Expense ratios are deducted from NAV over time; client redemptions force asset sales and can amplify trading costs and taxes.

list.title: Three sources
list.i1: Allocation effect: overweighting or underweighting an asset class
list.i2: Selection effect: stock picking within a class
list.i3: Fees and cash drag: expenses, taxes and uninvested cash

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: The portfolio returns 8% versus a 6% benchmark; 1.2% comes from a tech overweight and 0.8% from selection, with the rest from interaction and fees.
example.l2: A 0.75% annual fee can cost roughly 7%–8% of terminal value over ten years, depending on the return path.

key.title: Judge against the benchmark
key.text: High return is not proof of good management; evaluate against the mandate, benchmark and risk limits.

s4.title: Investment mandates and career path
s4.p1: A mandate defines the investable universe, benchmark, risk limits, liquidity requirements and reporting frequency; the manager is a fiduciary.
s4.p2: The usual path runs from analyst to portfolio manager to multi-strategy fund or fund founder. More senior roles own risk, attribution and client communication.

list.title: Four constraints
list.i1: Mandate and IPS: what may and may not be held
list.i2: Risk limits: volatility, drawdown and concentration caps
list.i3: Compliance and disclosure: records and conflicts

example.title: Scenario
example.l1: If the mandate prohibits leverage, a high-conviction stock must be bought with cash rather than margin.
example.l2: During a concentrated redemption, sell the most liquid assets first instead of dumping core holdings at the worst price.

key.title: Respect the boundary first
key.text: Stay inside the mandate, then pursue excess return; returns earned by breaking the boundary do not persist.

s1.title: Probability and statistics: from sample to conclusion
s1.p1: Returns are random variables. Describe them with mean, standard deviation, skew and correlation, then infer the population from a sample.
s1.p2: Sharpe ratio = (annual return − risk-free rate) / annual volatility. It measures excess return per unit of risk but ignores tail risk.

list.title: Three checks
list.i1: Sample size: short samples give unstable conclusions
list.i2: Distribution: returns are not normal and tails can be fat
list.i3: Survivorship bias: only surviving companies remain in the sample

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: With 12% return, 3% risk-free rate and 18% volatility, Sharpe = (12 − 3) / 18 = 0.5.
example.l2: The same return with 30% volatility gives Sharpe 0.3, a weaker risk-adjusted result.

key.title: Check the sample first
key.text: Ask whether the sample represents the population before trusting a metric; pretty data may come from a biased sample.

s2.title: Time series and backtesting
s2.p1: Time series analysis focuses on autocorrelation, volatility clustering and mean reversion; regressing non-stationary data can produce spurious relationships.
s2.p2: Backtests must avoid look-ahead bias, survivorship bias and ignored trading costs, then validate out-of-sample or with walk-forward tests.

list.title: Three biases
list.i1: Look-ahead bias: using information not available at the time
list.i2: Survivorship bias: only still-listed companies remain
list.i3: Trading costs: commissions, spreads and impact

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Generating today’s signal from the next 20 days of returns makes an absurdly good backtest that cannot be traded.
example.l2: Adding 0.1% cost and slippage per trade can turn a high-turnover strategy from profit to loss.

key.title: The purpose of a backtest
key.text: A backtest is for falsifying an idea early, not for proving it works; respect out-of-sample failure.

s3.title: Factor models and portfolio optimisation
s3.p1: Factor models split return into common exposures such as market, industry and style plus idiosyncratic return; alpha is what the factors cannot explain.
s3.p2: Portfolio optimisation trades expected return against risk and constraints such as no shorting, turnover and sector caps; estimation error gets amplified.

list.title: Three inputs
list.i1: Factor exposures: value, momentum, size and others
list.i2: Covariance matrix: how assets move together
list.i3: Constraints and turnover: real portfolios cannot adjust freely

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A portfolio has 0.8 value exposure and −0.3 momentum; it gains when value rebounds and loses when momentum persists.
example.l2: When covariance estimates are unstable, the optimiser can produce extreme weights; constraints and shrinkage help.

key.title: The optimiser is an amplifier
key.text: An optimiser amplifies your assumptions; bad estimates become extreme positions.

s4.title: Machine learning, overfitting and algorithmic trading
s4.p1: Machine learning can fit nonlinear relationships, but financial data has a low signal-to-noise ratio and is non-stationary, so overfitting risk is high.
s4.p2: Cross-validate by time, then monitor drift, trading costs and capacity after deployment.

list.title: Three disciplines
list.i1: Time-series cross-validation: never shuffle time
list.i2: Regularisation and simpler models: robustness before complexity
list.i3: Live monitoring and capacity: impact rises with capital

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A model with 90% training accuracy and 52% out-of-sample accuracy memorised noise rather than a pattern.
example.l2: Strategy capacity is limited: as capital grows, impact costs can consume the original alpha.

key.title: Out-of-sample first
key.text: Prove out-of-sample performance before discussing live trading; training performance has no decision value.

s1.title: Volatility smile and surface
s1.p1: Black-Scholes assumes one volatility, but the market quotes different implied volatilities for different strikes, creating a smile or skew.
s1.p2: Plotting IV across strikes and expiries gives the volatility surface; it reflects tail risk, supply and demand, and event expectations.

list.title: Three observations
list.i1: Skew: low-strike puts are usually more expensive
list.i2: Term structure: IV changes around events
list.i3: Surface arbitrage: neighbouring points should not offer riskless profit

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: For one expiry, a strike-80 put shows 35% IV while a strike-100 put shows 22%, a downward slope.
example.l2: Short-dated IV rises before earnings; if the move is small, IV falls afterwards and time value decays quickly.

key.title: Do not use one volatility
key.text: Do not price every strike with one volatility; the surface is the market’s actual quote structure.

s2.title: Greeks and dynamic hedging
s2.p1: Delta measures the option price change for a 1-unit move in the underlying; Gamma measures the change in Delta; Vega is volatility sensitivity and Theta is time sensitivity.
s2.p2: A delta-neutral book buys or sells the underlying to set total Delta to zero; as the underlying moves, the hedge must be rebalanced.

list.title: Three sensitivities
list.i1: Delta hedging: offset directional exposure
list.i2: Gamma risk: Delta changes as price moves
list.i3: Hedging cost: slippage, commissions and frequent adjustments

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Ten calls with 0.5 Delta and a 100 multiplier carry 500 shares of Delta; shorting 500 shares makes the book temporarily neutral.
example.l2: If Delta rises to 0.6 after a rally, short another 100 shares; frequent rebalancing creates costs.

key.title: Only instantaneously neutral
key.text: Delta neutrality is instantaneous; Gamma pulls the book away and requires continuous hedging.

s3.title: Gamma scalping and spreads
s3.p1: Buying options and dynamically delta hedging can profit when realised volatility exceeds implied volatility; this is gamma scalping.
s3.p2: Spread strategies combine different strikes or expiries to cap risk and reduce cost; calendar spreads are more sensitive to term structure.

list.title: Three structures
list.i1: Vertical spread: same expiry, different strikes
list.i2: Calendar spread: same strike, different expiries
list.i3: Ratio spread: unequal quantities

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A bull call spread long 95 and short 105 has maximum loss equal to net premium and capped maximum gain.
example.l2: A calendar spread long the front month and short the back month benefits when front-month IV falls relative to the back month.

key.title: Limited risk is not no risk
key.text: Spreads cap risk but also cap reward; do not treat limited risk as risk-free.

s4.title: Stress testing and career path
s4.p1: Derivative risk is nonlinear: when price, volatility, time and rates move together, the Greeks themselves change.
s4.p2: Stress tests should shock price and volatility together and include liquidity haircuts, higher margin and counterparty risk.

list.title: Three shocks
list.i1: Joint shocks: price and volatility move together
list.i2: Liquidity haircut: spreads widen under stress
list.i3: Model risk: assumptions fail and parameters become unstable

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: With the underlying down 10% and IV up 15 points, a short-put book can lose far more than a Delta-only estimate suggests.
example.l2: When volatility spikes, margin requirements rise and forced liquidation can amplify losses.

key.title: Test survival
key.text: A stress test is not a forecast; it checks whether the book survives the worst case.

s1.title: Corporate valuation and DCF
s1.p1: DCF discounts future free cash flow to today; the discount rate is usually WACC, reflecting the opportunity cost of equity and debt.
s1.p2: Terminal value often dominates a DCF; growth, margin and capex assumptions must be internally consistent.

list.title: Three inputs
list.i1: Cash flow forecast: revenue, margin and capex
list.i2: WACC: weighted cost of equity and debt
list.i3: Terminal value and sensitivity: perpetual growth or exit multiple

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Year-1 FCF of 100, 3% growth and 9% WACC give terminal value 100 × 1.03 / (0.09 − 0.03) = 1717.
