example.l2: Raising WACC from 9% to 10% cuts terminal value to 1471; valuation is highly sensitive to the discount rate.

key.title: Assumptions drive the output
key.text: DCF output quality depends on assumptions, not the formula; run sensitivity on the key inputs.

s2.title: Relative valuation and IPOs
s2.p1: Relative valuation uses comparable-company multiples such as P/E, EV/EBITDA or P/S to place the target inside a market pricing framework.
s2.p2: An IPO runs through preparation, roadshow, bookbuilding and pricing; the underwriter balances demand and valuation, and first-day premiums are common.

list.title: Three steps
list.i1: Comparable companies: similar business and growth
list.i2: Precedent transactions: multiples paid in M&A
list.i3: Bookbuilding and allocation: price from demand

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A peer average P/E of 18 and target EPS of 2 imply an indicative value near 36 per share.
example.l2: Pricing at 30 and closing at 36 on day one is a 20% first-day premium; the underwriter may have underestimated demand.

key.title: Relative, not absolute
key.text: Multiples give a relative price, not a guarantee of absolute value; peer selection drives the conclusion.

s3.title: Debt financing, M&A and dilution
s3.p1: Debt financing uses leverage to magnify shareholder returns but adds fixed interest and refinancing risk; leverage ratios and covenants are key constraints.
s3.p2: Whether an acquisition is EPS-accretive depends on synergies, financing and the exchange ratio; issuing new shares dilutes existing owners.

list.title: Three variables
list.i1: Leverage and interest coverage: can cash flow service debt?
list.i2: Synergies: can cost and revenue benefits be delivered?
list.i3: Exchange ratio and dilution: how many new shares are issued?

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Acquirer net income 100, target 30 and synergies 10; an all-stock deal issuing 20 new shares requires comparing merged EPS with standalone EPS.
example.l2: High-interest debt can offset synergies and turn an accretive deal into a dilutive one.

key.title: Accretion is not value creation
key.text: EPS accretion is not value creation; examine cash flow, risk and integration cost.

s4.title: Deal negotiation and career path
s4.p1: The IB deal process covers valuation, diligence, structuring, negotiation, board approval and closing; a fairness opinion supports the board’s decision.
s4.p2: The career path runs analyst → associate → vice president → director/managing director; modelling, industry insight and communication are core skills.

list.title: Three stages
list.i1: Deal structure: price, consideration and conditions
list.i2: Diligence and documents: representations, warranties and indemnities
list.i3: Negotiation and conflicts: who bears the risk?

example.title: Scenario
example.l1: A seller wants a higher price while a buyer demands stronger representations and warranties; the deal balances price against risk allocation.
example.l2: Advising both buyer and seller creates conflicts that must be disclosed or walled off.

key.title: Beyond price
key.text: Deals are not only about price; they also allocate and price risk.

s1.title: Monetary policy and interest rates
s1.p1: Central banks influence funding costs through policy rates, reserve requirements and asset purchases; cuts usually lower discount rates and support risk assets.
s1.p2: Transmission is lagged: corporate funding, mortgages, FX and asset prices react through different channels, sometimes over months.

list.title: Three variables
list.i1: Policy rate: the central bank’s short-rate anchor
list.i2: Inflation target: the anchor for policy reaction
list.i3: Transmission lag: from policy to the real economy and markets

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: A 50bp rate cut saves about 5,000 of annual interest on a 1m floating-rate loan.
example.l2: If inflation stays high, a cut can push long yields higher, steepen the curve and produce a mixed equity response.

key.title: Surprises drive prices
key.text: Policy direction is not market direction; prices respond to the surprise versus expectations, not headlines.

s2.title: Yield curve, inflation and government bonds
s2.p1: The yield curve connects government bond yields across maturities; a normal curve slopes upward, while inversion is often read as a recession signal.
s2.p2: Inflation expectations push nominal yields higher; real yield = nominal yield − expected inflation, affecting bond and equity valuation.

list.title: Three concepts
list.i1: Curve shape: normal, flat or inverted
list.i2: Breakeven inflation: the market’s inflation expectation
list.i3: Duration: sensitivity to yield changes

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Two-year 4.5% and ten-year 3.8% is a 70bp inversion; the market is pricing future cuts or a slowdown.
example.l2: A bond with duration 6 loses about 6% in price for a 1% rise in yield.

key.title: The curve contains expectations
key.text: The curve embeds growth and inflation expectations, not just the current rate; inversion is not a precise timing signal.

s3.title: FX and global capital flows
s3.p1: Exchange rates are driven by rate differentials, inflation, trade balances, capital flows and risk appetite; carry trades borrow in low-yield currencies and invest in high-yield ones.
s3.p2: When risk appetite falls, capital often returns to the dollar and safe assets, pressuring high-yield currencies and emerging markets.

list.title: Three drivers
list.i1: Rate differential: the gap between two countries’ rates
list.i2: Carry trade: borrow low-yield, invest high-yield
list.i3: Risk appetite: risk-on versus risk-off

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Borrowing at 1% to invest at 5% implies 4% annual carry, but a 5% currency depreciation turns it into a loss.
example.l2: In a global risk-off, a high-yield currency can suffer both narrowing rate differentials and capital outflows.

key.title: Carry is not free
key.text: Carry earns a premium for bearing tail risk; losses accelerate when the exchange rate reverses.

s4.title: Macro trading and career path
s4.p1: Macro traders judge the regime across growth, inflation, policy and liquidity, then express views through bonds, FX, equities or commodities.
s4.p2: The path runs macro research → strategist → macro fund or multi-asset portfolio manager; data interpretation, models and risk management matter.

list.title: Four dimensions
list.i1: Growth: expanding or slowing
list.i2: Inflation: rising or cooling
list.i3: Policy: easing or tightening

example.title: Scenario
example.l1: With slower growth, cooling inflation and a dovish central bank, a portfolio may overweight long-duration bonds and underweight cyclicals.
example.l2: If cuts are fully priced, assets can still fall on the news as the market sells the fact.

key.title: Express the view
key.text: A macro view must be expressed through assets, with exits and risk controls for being wrong.

s1.title: Order book and bid-ask spread
s1.p1: The order book ranks limit orders by price then time; the gap between the best bid and best ask is the spread.
s1.p2: A market order crosses the spread and pays for immediacy; a limit order provides liquidity but may not fill.

list.title: Three concepts
list.i1: Best bid and ask: the closest quotes
list.i2: Depth: quantity available at each price
list.i3: Queue position: order priority at the same price

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: Bid 99.95 and ask 100.05 give a 0.10 spread; buying 100 shares immediately costs about 10 extra.
example.l2: An order larger than the best-level depth walks to worse prices and creates impact cost.

key.title: Liquidity has a price
key.text: The spread is the price of immediacy; liquidity is not free, so trade off waiting against certainty.

s2.title: Market makers and liquidity
s2.p1: Market makers quote both bid and ask to earn the spread while bearing inventory and adverse-selection risk.
s2.p2: When inventory deviates from target, they skew quotes or hedge; informed traders pick off their quotes.

list.title: Three risks
list.i1: Inventory risk: holding unwanted positions
list.i2: Adverse selection: being filled by informed traders
list.i3: Quote skewing: using prices to manage inventory

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: After buying 10,000 shares, a long-inventory maker may lower the bid and raise the ask to encourage selling.
example.l2: If the counterparty has bullish information, the price rises right after the maker buys and the spread is eaten by adverse selection.

key.title: The spread compensates risk
key.text: Market-maker profit compensates for risk and liquidity provision; it is not risk-free income.

s3.title: Price impact and algorithmic execution
s3.p1: Large orders consume order-book depth and move prices; impact cost varies with size, speed and liquidity.
s3.p2: Execution algorithms slice large orders into child orders, using VWAP, TWAP or participation rates to balance impact against timing risk.

list.title: Three tools
list.i1: Impact model: size, volatility and depth
list.i2: VWAP/TWAP: slice by volume or time
list.i3: Participation rate: control your share of market volume

example.title: Worked example
example.l1: With daily volume of 1m shares and a 100k order, a 10% participation rate needs about one trading day.
example.l2: Rushing raises impact cost; waiting too long exposes the order to price drift and news risk.

key.title: Impact versus time
key.text: Optimal execution trades impact cost against timing risk; no single algorithm is always best.

s4.title: Market quality and career path
s4.p1: Market quality is measured by spreads, depth, speed, price stability and trading costs; fragmented markets add routing complexity.
s4.p2: The path runs trader → execution consultant → market-structure research or market making; rules, data and matching engines matter.

list.title: Three dimensions
list.i1: Fragmentation: one stock traded in many venues
list.i2: High-frequency trading: speed and liquidity as a double-edged sword
list.i3: Regulation and fairness: how rules shape execution

example.title: Scenario
example.l1: With the same stock quoted in several venues, a router must choose the best execution while avoiding information leakage.
example.l2: High-frequency market making adds liquidity in calm markets but can withdraw quickly under stress, amplifying volatility.

key.title: Liquidity is state-dependent
key.text: Liquidity is state-dependent: abundant in calm markets and can vanish under stress.

q1.prompt: Which description of a stock is most accurate?
q1.o1: A share of ownership in a company
q1.o2: A loan made to a company
q1.o4: A contract that guarantees a return
q1.explain: A stock represents part-ownership of a company. Lending money to a company and expecting repayment describes a bond, not a stock.

q2.prompt: What is the formula for market capitalisation?
q2.explain: Market cap measures the whole company's market value: the share price multiplied by every share the company has issued.

q3.prompt: A fictional company trades at {price} and has {shares} million shares outstanding. What is its market cap in millions of USD?
q3.work: Market cap = price × shares = {price} × {shares} million shares = {answer} million USD.
q3.explain: Treat shares outstanding as millions of shares; multiplying gives the answer directly in millions of USD.

q4.prompt: “A lower share price always means a cheaper stock.” Is this statement true or false?
q4.explain: A low share price does not mean cheap. Judge value using market cap, earnings and share count. A $5 stock can be more expensive than a $500 stock.

q5.prompt: Which of these are basic rights of an ordinary shareholder?
q5.o1: Voting in proportion to shares owned
q5.o2: Receiving dividends when the company pays them
q5.o3: Demanding the company return your principal at any time
q5.o4: Selling your shares to someone else
q5.explain: Shareholders have voting, dividend and transfer rights. Demanding principal back at any time is a feature of bonds or deposits.

q6.prompt: What is the main purpose of a ticker symbol?
q6.o1: To identify a specific company on an exchange
q6.o2: To determine a fair share price
q6.o3: To show how large the company is
q6.o4: To guarantee that dividends are paid
q6.explain: A ticker is an identifier used to specify a company in markets and orders. It says nothing about price, size or dividends.

q1.prompt: At what price does a market buy order usually fill?
q1.o1: The last traded price
q1.o2: The best current ask
q1.explain: As a buyer you trade against a seller, so a market buy usually fills at the ask.

q2.prompt: Your account has {cash} cash, the ask is {price}, and each order costs {fee} in commission. What is the largest whole number of shares you can buy?
q2.explain: Cash must cover both the trade and the commission. Subtract the fee, divide by the price, then round down to a whole share.

q3.prompt: Your total equity (cash + position value) increases immediately after buying a stock. True or false?
q3.explain: Ignoring fees, total equity is unchanged: cash simply becomes stock. Fees reduce total equity slightly.

q4.prompt: Which of these are trading costs?
q4.o4: Slippage away from the expected price
q4.explain: Commissions, spreads and slippage all reduce your effective return. A rising price is a source of gain, not a cost.

q5.prompt: Which statement about the bid and ask is correct?
q5.o1: The ask is usually above the bid, and the spread is a trading cost
q5.o2: The bid is usually above the ask
q5.o4: A wider spread means lower trading costs
q5.explain: The bid is the highest buyer price; the ask is the lowest seller price. Normally the ask is above the bid, and a wider spread costs more.

q6.prompt: A stock has a bid of {bid} and an ask of {ask}. You buy {qty} shares at the ask and immediately sell at the bid, ignoring commission. What is the loss caused by the spread in USD?
q6.explain: You pay the ask and receive the bid. The difference times the quantity is the round-trip spread cost.

q1.prompt: What does “unrealized P&L” mean?
q1.o1: Profit or loss already locked into cash after selling
q1.o2: Paper profit or loss on an unsold position that moves with the price
q1.o3: Net income reported by the company
q1.explain: Unrealized P&L is the floating gain or loss while you still hold shares. It becomes realized only when you sell.

q2.prompt: You buy {n1} shares at {p1}, then {n2} shares at {p2}, with no fees. What is the average cost in USD?
q2.explain: Average cost is a weighted average: total cost divided by total shares, not a simple average of the two prices.

q3.prompt: You buy {qty} shares at {buy}, sell at {sell}, and pay {fee} commission on each side. What is the net profit in USD?
q3.explain: Net profit is the gross price gain minus both the buy and sell commissions.

q4.prompt: If the selling price is above the purchase price, the trade is always profitable after fees. True or false?
q4.explain: Not necessarily. A small price gain can be wiped out by commissions. Judge by net profit.

q5.o1: Realized P&L happens after a sale
q5.o2: Unrealized P&L changes with the share price
q5.o3: Paper gains are cash you already hold
q5.explain: Realized P&L is locked in on sale; unrealized P&L moves with price; paper gains are not cash; commissions directly reduce net profit.

q6.prompt: What is the correct way to calculate return?
q6.explain: Return measures P&L relative to the capital invested: P&L ÷ cost × 100%.

q1.prompt: What usually happens to a buy limit placed below the market price?
q1.o1: It waits until the price falls to the limit or lower before filling
q1.o2: It fills immediately at the market price
q1.o3: It fills above the market price
q1.explain: A buy limit fills only when the ask reaches the limit or lower, so it typically rests in the order book first.

q2.prompt: You place a buy limit for {qty} shares at {limit} with a {fee} commission. How much cash must be reserved?
q2.explain: A buy limit reserves quantity × limit price plus any commission.

q3.prompt: A limit order guarantees execution. True or false?
q3.explain: Limit orders guarantee a price, not a fill. If the market never reaches your limit, the order waits.

q4.prompt: Which of these are risks of market orders?
q4.o2: Slippage is possible in volatile conditions
q4.o4: You cannot lock the execution price
q4.explain: Market orders prioritise execution, so price is uncertain and slippage is possible. Never filling is a typical limit-order risk.

q5.prompt: What does the order status “open” mean?
q5.o2: The order is submitted and waiting for its price condition
q5.explain: Open means the order is still working in the order book, waiting to fill or be cancelled.

q6.prompt: A stock has a bid of {bid} and an ask of {ask}. You buy {qty} shares at the ask and immediately sell at the bid. What is the spread cost in USD?
q6.explain: As with a market order: you pay the ask and receive the bid, and the difference times quantity is the cost.

q1.prompt: Which statement best describes a cash dividend?
q1.o1: The company distributes part of its profits to shareholders in cash
q1.o2: A dividend is the gain from a rising share price
q1.o3: Any profitable company must pay a dividend
q1.explain: A dividend is cash distributed by the company from profits and cash flow. Whether and how much to pay is a company decision.

q2.prompt: You hold {qty} shares and the dividend is {perShare} per share. How much cash do you receive?
q2.explain: The cash dividend equals shares held times dividend per share. Your purchase cost does not change the payment.

q3.prompt: In the simplified ex-dividend model, what usually happens to the share price on the ex-date?
q3.o2: It adjusts down by roughly the dividend per share
q3.o3: It does not change at all
q3.explain: Cash leaves the company, so the price usually adjusts down by about the dividend. You gain cash but the position value falls.

q4.prompt: Which statements about dividend yield are correct?
q4.o1: It equals annual dividend per share ÷ current price
q4.o2: A falling share price can raise the yield
q4.o3: The yield is a guaranteed return
q4.o4: A very high yield may not be sustainable
q4.explain: Yield moves with price; a falling price raises it. It is not guaranteed, and a high yield can reflect risk or an unsustainable payout.

q5.prompt: What does the payout ratio measure?
q5.o3: Dividend per share ÷ earnings per share
q5.explain: Payout ratio = dividend per share ÷ EPS. It shows how much of earnings the company distributes.

q6.prompt: Annual dividend per share is {annual} and the share price is {price}. What is the dividend yield in percent?
q6.explain: The yield converts the annual dividend per share into a percentage of the share price; price changes move the yield.

q1.prompt: What is the most typical feature of a growth stock?
q1.o1: Revenue and earnings grow above average and profits are usually reinvested
q1.o2: It pays a high fixed dividend
q1.o3: Its earnings move exactly with the economic cycle
q1.o4: Its price is always below book value
q1.explain: Growth stocks are defined by growth rather than current income. They often reinvest profits, so dividends are low.

q2.prompt: Why might a value stock be cheap?
q2.o1: The market may be undervaluing it, or fundamentals may be deteriorating
q2.o2: It is guaranteed to go bankrupt
q2.o4: It must have the fastest growth
q2.explain: A low valuation can come from a market misunderstanding or from real fundamental problems. Cheap alone is not a reason to buy.

q3.prompt: Which statement about cyclical stocks is correct?
q3.o1: Their earnings are closely tied to the economic cycle
q3.o3: They are completely unaffected by rates and demand
q3.explain: Cyclical earnings swing with expansions and recessions; they are common in industrials, materials and energy.

q4.prompt: Which statements about stock style labels are correct?
q4.o1: A style label is a starting point, not a return guarantee
q4.o2: A company's style can change over time
q4.o3: A high dividend always means low risk
q4.o4: Growth stocks can also suffer large drawdowns
q4.explain: Style describes characteristics; companies change, high yields may not last, and growth valuations can fall sharply.

q1.prompt: Which description of an ETF is most accurate?
q1.o1: A long-term bond from a single company
q1.o2: A basket of assets traded on an exchange
q1.o3: A fund that can only be bought off-exchange
q1.o4: A product that guarantees principal and return
q1.explain: ETFs trade like stocks, but the underlying is a basket of assets, usually tracking an index, sector or theme.

q2.prompt: What risk does diversification mainly reduce?
q2.explain: Diversification softens individual company or sector shocks, but cannot remove overall market risk.

q3.prompt: Which statements about diversification are correct?
q3.o2: More holdings is not always better
q3.o4: Sector ETFs can still be highly concentrated
q3.explain: Diversification depends on correlation; over-diversifying adds complexity; systematic risk remains; sector ETFs are concentrated bets.

q4.prompt: {weight}% of a portfolio returns {r1} and the rest returns {r2}. What is the portfolio return in percent?
q4.explain: Portfolio return is the weighted average of asset returns; the weights sum to 100%.

q1.prompt: What is the main difference between compound and simple interest?
q1.o1: Compound interest is paid only on the original principal
q1.o2: Compound interest adds interest to principal so it earns further interest
q1.o4: They always produce the same result
q1.explain: Compounding reinvests interest: each period's interest becomes part of the next period's principal.

q2.prompt: Principal is {principal}, the annual return is {rate}%, compounded annually for {years} years. What is the future value in USD?
q2.explain: Future value equals principal times (1 + annual return) raised to the number of years, assuming all interest is reinvested.

q3.prompt: Which statement about time and compounding is correct?
q3.o1: Longer horizons amplify compounding, but risk does not disappear
q3.o2: Longer horizons guarantee a positive return
q3.o3: Time has no effect on compounding
q3.explain: Time magnifies both compounding and uncertainty; long-term investing can still suffer losses and drawdowns.

q4.prompt: Which statements about long-term investing are correct?
q4.o1: Inflation reduces the purchasing power of cash and returns
q4.o2: A 50% fall requires a 100% gain to recover
q4.explain: Inflation, drawdowns and fees all affect real outcomes; history does not guarantee future performance.

q1.prompt: Which two prices form the body of a candlestick?
q1.o1: Open and close
q1.o2: High and low
q1.explain: The body connects open and close; the wicks extend to the high and low.

q2.prompt: A candle whose close is above its open is usually called what?
q2.explain: Close above open is bullish (green in this game); close below open is bearish (red).

q3.prompt: Which statements about candles and volume are correct?
q3.o2: Volume reflects trading activity in the period
q3.o3: One candle can accurately predict the future
q3.o4: Shapes must be read with trend and location
q3.explain: Timeframe, volume and trend location all matter; a single candle cannot accurately predict the future.

q4.prompt: A session opens at {open} and closes at {close}. What is the candle body size in USD?
q4.explain: Body size is the absolute difference between open and close, independent of high and low.

q1.prompt: What does SMA20 mean?
q1.o1: The arithmetic average of the last 20 closes
q1.o2: The highest price of the last 20 days
q1.o3: The close of the 20th trading day
q1.o4: A forecast of the next 20 days
q1.explain: SMA is a simple moving average of the last N closes and never uses future data.

q2.prompt: RSI above 70 usually indicates what?
q2.o3: Strong recent upward momentum; possibly overbought
q2.explain: RSI above 70 shows strong recent gains and possible overbought conditions; strong trends can stay high.

q3.prompt: Which statements about technical indicators are correct?
q3.o1: They are computed from history and lag
q3.o4: They help confirm trends and manage risk
q3.explain: Indicators describe and lag; parameters matter; they cannot guarantee profits.

q4.prompt: The last three closes are {p1}, {p2} and {p3}. What is SMA3 in USD?
q4.explain: A simple moving average is the arithmetic average of the last N closes.

q1.prompt: In the income statement, how is net income typically derived?
q1.o1: Revenue minus costs and expenses
q1.o2: Assets minus liabilities
q1.explain: The income statement starts with revenue, subtracts operating costs, expenses and taxes, and ends with net income.

q2.prompt: What is the fundamental balance-sheet identity?
q2.explain: Assets are financed by liabilities and equity, so assets = liabilities + equity.

q3.prompt: Which statements about earnings quality are correct?
q3.o1: Net income is not the same as cash
q3.o2: Free cash flow can fund dividends, buybacks and debt repayment
q3.explain: Profit needs cash support; FCF is a key source; too much debt raises risk; margin trends reveal operating quality.

q4.prompt: A company has revenue of {revenue}M and cost of goods sold of {cogs}M. What is gross profit in millions?
q4.explain: Gross profit is revenue minus cost of goods sold, the first step of the income statement.

q1.prompt: What is the core idea of DCF valuation?
q1.o1: Multiply the current price by shares
q1.o2: Discount future free cash flow to today's value
q1.o3: Use the historical high as value
q1.o4: Use book value instead of market value
q1.explain: DCF discounts future cash flow at a risk-adjusted rate to estimate enterprise value.

q2.prompt: All else equal, what happens to a DCF valuation if the discount rate rises?
q2.o4: Value per share must be zero
q2.explain: A higher discount rate reduces the present value of future cash flow, so the valuation falls.

q3.prompt: Which statements about DCF assumptions are correct?
q3.o1: Growth and discount rate are highly sensitive inputs
q3.o2: Terminal value can dominate enterprise value
q3.o3: DCF gives an exact real value to the cent
q3.o4: Perpetual growth must stay below the discount rate
q3.explain: DCF is highly assumption-sensitive and terminal-heavy; it is not an exact answer; the perpetual model requires r > g.

q4.prompt: Next year's free cash flow is {fcf}M, the discount rate is {discount}%, and there is no terminal value. What is the present value in millions?
q4.explain: Cash flow one year ahead is discounted by (1+r) to today's value.

q1.prompt: What does GDP measure?
q1.o1: The total output of an economy
q1.o2: A company's net income
q1.o3: The total market cap of the stock market
q1.o4: Cash held by the central bank
q1.explain: GDP, gross domestic product, measures the total output of an economy over a period.

q2.prompt: How does rising inflation usually affect the purchasing power of cash?
q2.explain: Higher prices mean the same amount buys less, so cash purchasing power falls.

q3.prompt: Which statements about rates and valuation are correct?
q3.o1: Rate hikes usually raise the discount rate and lower valuations
q3.o2: High-growth stocks are more sensitive to the discount rate
q3.o3: Rates have no effect on equity valuation
q3.o4: Rate cuts usually support risk assets
q3.explain: Higher discount rates reduce present values; growth stocks have longer duration and are more sensitive; cuts ease financial conditions.

q4.prompt: Policy rate 3%, inflation 4%. What is the real rate?
q4.explain: Real rate = nominal rate − inflation = 3% − 4% = −1%.

q1.prompt: What does asset allocation mainly determine?
q1.o1: The portfolio's risk and return structure
q1.o2: The name of a single stock
q1.explain: Weights across asset classes determine expected return, volatility and the sources of risk.

q2.prompt: Which situation usually gives better diversification?
q2.o2: All assets in the same sector
q2.explain: Lower correlation means assets are less likely to fall together, so portfolio volatility usually improves.

q3.prompt: Which statements about portfolio construction are correct?
q3.o1: A very large single position magnifies drawdowns
q3.o2: Rebalancing can restore the intended risk exposure
q3.explain: Concentration increases risk; rebalancing controls drift; over-diversification adds cost; correlations change.

q4.prompt: {stock}% of assets return {stockReturn} and the rest return {bondReturn}. What is the portfolio return in percent?
q4.explain: Portfolio return is the weighted average of asset returns.

q1.prompt: What is the basic position-sizing formula?
q1.o1: Risk amount ÷ risk per share
q1.o2: Account balance ÷ share price
q1.explain: Take the risk you can accept and divide it by the per-share risk (entry minus stop) to get shares.

q2.prompt: After a 50% fall, what gain is needed to get back to the starting value?
q2.explain: From 100 down to 50, recovering to 100 requires a 100% gain.

q3.prompt: Which statements about risk management are correct?
q3.o1: Highly correlated positions should be combined when measuring risk
q3.o2: Stops can be jumped by gaps
q3.explain: Correlated risk adds up; stops have gap risk; leverage magnifies risk; drawdown control protects long-term compounding.

q4.prompt: Account {account}, risk per trade {risk}%, entry {entry}, stop {stop}. How many shares should you buy?
q4.work: Risk amount = {account} × {risk}%; risk per share = {entry} − {stop}; shares = risk amount ÷ risk per share (rounded down) = {answer}.
q4.explain: Shares = risk amount ÷ risk per share, rounded down to whole shares.

q1.prompt: What does a value strategy typically look for?
q1.o1: Assets priced low relative to fundamentals
q1.o2: Assets with the strongest recent rally
q1.o3: The largest companies by market cap
q1.explain: Value focuses on opportunities that are cheap relative to earnings, assets or cash flow.

q2.prompt: What is the core assumption of momentum?
q2.explain: Momentum assumes recent strength persists, buying winners and selling losers.

q3.prompt: Which statements about strategy backtests are correct?
q3.o3: Strong in-sample results guarantee future performance
q3.explain: Backtests need no look-ahead, out-of-sample testing and cost assumptions; in-sample performance is not a guarantee.

q4.prompt: What does a dividend strategy mainly focus on?
q4.explain: Dividend strategies focus on cash returns, but must check whether the payout is sustainable.

q1.prompt: What is the basic sequence of a short sale?
q1.o1: Buy shares and wait for a rally
q1.o2: Borrow shares, sell them, then buy them back and return them
q1.o4: Issue new shares to the company
q1.explain: A short sells borrowed shares first, then buys them back cheaper; the difference is the gross profit.

q2.prompt: What is the defining risk of a short position?
q2.o2: The maximum loss equals the collateral
q2.o3: Losses are unlimited as the price rises
q2.o4: It can only be held for one day
q2.explain: A price can theoretically rise without limit, so short losses have no ceiling.

q3.prompt: Which costs can a short position create?
q3.explain: Borrowing costs a fee, dividends must be paid, and collateral is tied up.

q4.prompt: Short {qty} shares at {entry}, then cover at {exit}. Ignoring fees, what is the realised P&L in dollars?
q4.explain: Short P&L = (sale price − repurchase price) × shares.

q1.prompt: What is the core purpose of a margin account?
q1.o1: Removing commissions
q1.o2: Borrowing cash or securities to enlarge positions
q1.explain: A margin account borrows cash or securities, enlarging both gains and losses.

q2.prompt: How is financing interest normally charged?
q2.o2: Daily on the debit balance at an annual rate
q2.o3: Only when the position is profitable
q2.o4: It does not depend on holding time
q2.explain: Interest accrues daily as debit balance × annual rate ÷ trading days.

q3.prompt: Which factors raise financing cost?
q3.explain: Balance, rate and time all raise cost; lower volatility does not.

q4.prompt: A debit balance of {debit} carries an 8% annual rate with 252 trading days. What is the daily financing interest in dollars?
q4.explain: Interest = debit balance × annual rate ÷ trading days.

q1.prompt: When does a sell stop order normally trigger?
q1.o1: When the price is above the stop
q1.o2: When the price is at or below the stop
q1.o4: When the company pays a dividend
q1.explain: A sell stop protects a long and becomes a market sell when the trigger is crossed.

q2.prompt: What is the key difference between a trailing stop and a plain stop?
q2.o1: A trailing stop has no trigger
q2.o2: A trailing stop tightens as the price moves favourably
q2.o3: A trailing stop guarantees the fill price
q2.o4: A trailing stop only works after hours
q2.explain: A trailing stop follows favourable prices and never loosens.

q3.prompt: Which execution problems can stop orders face?
q3.o3: Guaranteed fills at the stop price
q3.explain: Stops do not guarantee price; gaps, thin books and clustering widen slippage.

q4.prompt: Buy at {entry} and set a trailing stop with a {trail} dollar trail. Before any price move, what is the initial stop price?
q4.explain: A trailing stop starts the configured distance below the entry price.

q1.prompt: What is the bid-ask spread in an order book?
q1.o1: The day high minus the day low
q1.o2: The best ask minus the best bid
q1.explain: Spread = best ask − best bid, the immediate cost of trading.

q2.prompt: Why does a large market order suffer slippage?
q2.o1: Visible depth is too thin, so it consumes several levels
q2.explain: The order walks multiple levels, so the average fill moves away from the best quote.

q3.prompt: Which practices reduce market impact?
q3.o3: Sending the whole order at market at once
q3.explain: Slicing, limits and spreading execution reduce impact on visible depth.

q4.prompt: Best ask {best} holds {size1} shares and the next ask {second} holds {size2}. Buying {qty} shares (best level first) gives what average price?
q4.explain: A large order fills level by level; the average is the size-weighted price.

q1.prompt: What is the core right of an option buyer?
q1.o1: The right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell at the strike
q1.o2: The obligation to buy at the strike
q1.explain: The buyer pays a premium for a right and can choose whether to exercise.

q2.prompt: A standard US equity option usually covers how many shares?
q2.explain: The standard multiplier is 100 shares: premiums are quoted per share but settle on 100.

q3.prompt: Which terms define an option contract?
q3.explain: Underlying, strike, expiry and premium together define the contract.

q4.prompt: At expiry the underlying is {spot} and the strike is {strike}. What is the call’s intrinsic value per share?
q4.explain: A call’s intrinsic value is max(spot − strike, 0).

q1.prompt: When does a long call profit at expiry?
q1.o1: When the stock is above the strike
q1.o2: When the stock is above the strike plus the premium per share
q1.o3: When the stock is below the strike
q1.o4: Whenever the stock rises at all
q1.explain: The stock must clear the breakeven of strike plus premium.

q2.prompt: What is the maximum loss on a long call?
q2.explain: A long call can lose at most the premium and commission paid.

q3.prompt: Which factors usually raise a call premium?
q3.explain: Higher spot, higher volatility and more time all raise call value.

q4.prompt: Strike {strike} with a premium of {premium} per share. What is the call breakeven?
q4.explain: Call breakeven = strike + premium per share.

q1.prompt: What right does a put buyer hold?
q1.o1: To sell the underlying at the strike
q1.o2: To buy the underlying at the strike
q1.explain: A put gives the buyer the right to sell at the strike.

q2.prompt: When does a long put profit at expiry?
q2.o1: When the stock is above the strike
q2.o2: When the stock is below the strike minus the premium per share
q2.o3: When the stock equals the strike
q2.o4: Whenever the stock falls at all
q2.explain: The stock must fall below the breakeven of strike minus premium.

q3.prompt: What can a long put be used for?
q3.explain: Puts hedge, speculate on declines and insure; they do not raise dividends.

q4.prompt: Strike {strike} with a premium of {premium} per share. What is the put breakeven?
q4.explain: Put breakeven = strike − premium per share.

q1.prompt: As expiry approaches, what usually happens to an option’s time value?
q1.o1: It decays toward zero
q1.o2: It rises steadily
q1.explain: Time value decays toward expiry; theta is negative for long options.

q2.prompt: Higher implied volatility usually does what to call and put premiums?
q2.explain: Higher volatility raises uncertainty and the time value of both calls and puts.

q3.prompt: Which statements about the Greeks are correct?
q3.o1: Delta measures the premium change for a $1 move in the underlying
q3.o2: Gamma measures how fast delta changes
q3.o3: Theta is usually negative for buyers and represents time decay
q3.o4: Vega measures the impact of a change in the strike
q3.explain: Delta, gamma and theta are described correctly; vega measures volatility sensitivity, not strike changes.

q4.prompt: A call with spot {spot}, strike {strike} trades at {premium}. What is its time value?
q4.explain: Time value = premium − intrinsic value.

q1.prompt: What is the core obligation of an option seller?
q1.o1: None; the seller just keeps the premium
q1.o2: To perform when the buyer exercises
q1.explain: Sellers collect premium but must perform if the buyer exercises.

q2.prompt: What is the maximum profit on a short call?
q2.explain: A short option’s maximum profit is the premium received.

q3.prompt: Which risks or requirements come with selling options?
q3.explain: Selling needs collateral, can be assigned and can lose more than the premium.

q4.prompt: Sell one {strike} call for {premium}. At expiry the stock is {spot}. Ignoring fees, what is the P&L in dollars?
q4.explain: Seller P&L = premium received − intrinsic value × 100.

q1.prompt: What makes up a covered call?
q1.o1: Short 100 shares + long call
q1.o2: Long 100 shares + short one call
q1.explain: A covered call uses 100 shares to cover one short call.

q2.prompt: What is the maximum profit on a cash-secured put?
q2.explain: A CSP’s maximum profit is the premium received.

q3.prompt: Which statements about covered calls are correct?
q3.o3: The stock still carries downside risk
q3.explain: Covered calls add income and cap upside but do not remove stock downside.

q4.prompt: Cash-secured put: strike {strike}, premium {premium}. What is the maximum loss in dollars?
q4.explain: CSP maximum loss = (strike − premium) × 100.

q1.prompt: Which legs form a bull call spread?
q1.o1: Sell lower-strike call + buy higher-strike call
q1.o2: Buy lower-strike call + sell higher-strike call
q1.explain: Bull call spread = buy lower-strike call + sell higher-strike call.

q2.prompt: What is the usual maximum loss on a vertical spread?
q2.explain: A debit spread’s maximum loss is normally the net debit paid.

q3.prompt: What are the advantages of spreads?
q3.o2: Lower premium than a single leg
q3.explain: Spreads define risk, reduce cost and clarify payoffs, but cap profit.

q4.prompt: A bull call spread has a strike width of {width} and a net debit of {debit}. What is the maximum profit in dollars for one contract?
q4.explain: Spread maximum profit = (strike width − net debit) × 100.

q1.prompt: Which legs form a long straddle?
q1.o1: Sell a same-strike call + sell a same-strike put
q1.o2: Buy a same-strike call + put with the same expiry
q1.explain: A straddle buys a call and a put at the same strike and expiry.

q2.prompt: How does a long strangle differ from a straddle?
q2.o2: It uses different strikes and costs less
q2.explain: A strangle buys out-of-the-money calls and puts at different strikes for less premium.

q3.prompt: When do long-volatility strategies have an edge?
q3.o1: A large move is expected in either direction
q3.o3: An event could trigger violent movement
q3.o4: The market is expected to stay flat for months
q3.explain: Long volatility needs a large move or a low starting volatility; flat markets hurt.

q4.prompt: A {strike} straddle costs {callPremium} for the call and {putPremium} for the put. What is the upper breakeven?
q4.explain: Straddle upper breakeven = strike + both premiums.

q1.prompt: What is the core feature of a futures contract?
q1.o1: An agreement to trade the underlying at a set price on a future date
q1.o2: Immediate stock delivery
q1.explain: Futures lock in a future price and carry directional risk.

q2.prompt: How does margin affect futures risk?
q2.o2: Margin is only part of notional while P&L uses full notional
q2.explain: Margin is collateral; P&L uses full notional, so leverage amplifies risk.

q3.prompt: Which mechanisms are part of futures trading?
q3.o2: Cash settlement or delivery at expiry
q3.explain: Futures involve daily settlement, expiry and margin; profit is never guaranteed.

q4.prompt: Open one long future at {entry} and settle at {exit}, multiplier 100. What is the P&L in dollars?
q4.explain: Long futures P&L = (settlement − entry) × contracts × 100.

q1.prompt: How do you hedge a long stock position with futures?
q1.o1: Go long futures
q1.o2: Short an equivalent futures notional
q1.explain: Short futures offset the stock’s downside direction.

q2.prompt: What does a 0.5 hedge ratio mean?
q2.explain: The hedge ratio sets the share of notional to short.

q3.prompt: Which residual risks can remain after hedging?
q3.explain: Hedging lowers direction risk but leaves basis, correlation and margin risk.

q4.prompt: Hold {shares} shares at {price}; each futures contract covers 100 shares at {price}. How many contracts fully hedge 1:1?
q4.explain: Each contract covers 100 shares, so shares ÷ 100 gives the contract count.

q1.prompt: What is a liquidity spiral in a crisis?
q1.o1: Forced selling pushes prices down and triggers more liquidation
q1.o2: Everyone buys at once
q1.explain: Declines force sales, which deepen declines and cause more selling.

q2.prompt: What usually happens to correlations in a crisis?
q2.explain: Correlations rise under stress, weakening diversification.

q3.prompt: Which practices help survive a crisis?
q3.explain: Cash, lower leverage and diversification are survival basics.

q4.prompt: Equity {equity}, leverage {leverage}x, a {shock}% decline. What is the approximate loss in dollars?
q4.explain: Leverage amplifies the shock: equity × leverage × decline.

q1.prompt: What is the core requirement of the final challenge?
q1.o1: Make the most money
q1.o2: Complete real stock, option and futures trades while keeping the account alive
q1.explain: The challenge is cross-tool execution and risk management, not just returns.

q2.prompt: How should a per-trade risk budget be set?
q2.o1: Set maximum loss first, then size the position
q2.explain: Define maximum loss and stop distance, then compute size.

q3.prompt: What belongs in a trading plan?
q3.explain: Plans cover thesis, tools, risk and review, never guaranteed profit.

q4.prompt: Account {account}, risk {risk}%, entry {entry}, stop {stop}. How many shares should you buy?
q4.work: Risk amount = {account} × {risk}%; risk per share = {entry} − {stop}; shares = risk amount ÷ risk per share = {answer}.
q4.explain: Shares = risk amount ÷ risk per share, rounded down.

q1.prompt: What is the correct formula for fund NAV?
q1.o1: Total assets / shares
q1.o2: (Asset value − liabilities) / shares
q1.explain: NAV is per-share net value: subtract liabilities, then divide by shares.

q2.prompt: What usually happens after a large subscription?
q2.o3: AUM rises, but NAV does not change from the subscription itself
q2.explain: A subscription adds shares and assets at NAV, so AUM grows while NAV itself does not change from the subscription alone.

q3.prompt: What is the core of risk budgeting?
q3.o1: Allocate by risk contribution, not only by capital weight
q3.explain: Risk budgeting looks at each position’s contribution to portfolio volatility.

q4.prompt: A 60/40 portfolio drifts to 70% stocks. Disciplined rebalancing usually means:
q4.o4: Sell some stocks and buy bonds
q4.explain: Rebalancing pulls weights back to the target range.

q5.prompt: In attribution, return from overweighting the technology sector is:
q5.explain: Allocation effect comes from deviations in asset-class or sector weights.

q6.prompt: When evaluating a fund, which items should be considered together?
q6.explain: Size is not performance; look at relative return, risk and cost.

q1.prompt: What is look-ahead bias?
q1.o1: Using only historical prices
q1.o2: Ignoring trading costs
q1.o3: Using information that was unavailable at the time
q1.explain: Look-ahead bias lets a backtest see the future, which cannot be reproduced live.

q2.prompt: Survivorship bias most often appears when:
q2.o2: Analysing only companies that survive today
q2.explain: Delisted or bankrupt companies are excluded, overstating historical returns.

q3.prompt: What is the numerator of the Sharpe ratio?
q3.o1: Annual return minus the risk-free rate
q3.explain: Sharpe measures excess return per unit of volatility.

q4.prompt: What is the classic sign of overfitting?
q4.o1: Good in and out of sample
q4.o2: Bad in sample, good out of sample
q4.o4: Very good in sample, much worse out of sample
q4.explain: The model memorises training noise and deteriorates out of sample.

q5.prompt: In a factor model, alpha usually means:
q5.o2: Excess return not explained by factors
q5.explain: Alpha is the residual return beyond factor exposures.

q6.explain: Backtests should try to falsify the idea rather than pick the prettiest curve.

q1.prompt: What is the volatility smile?
q1.o1: All strikes have the same IV
q1.o2: Different strikes have different implied volatilities
q1.o3: Historical volatility is always below implied
q1.o4: Option prices change linearly with expiry
q1.explain: The market quotes different implied volatilities for different strikes.

q2.prompt: Delta measures:
q2.o1: The option price change for a 1-unit underlying move
q2.o2: The option price change for a 1-point volatility move
q2.o4: The change for a 1% rate move
q2.explain: Delta is the first-order sensitivity of option price to the underlying.

q3.prompt: The core of gamma scalping is:
q3.o3: Dynamic delta hedging to profit when realised volatility exceeds implied
q3.explain: Repeated delta hedging converts realised volatility into P&L.

q4.prompt: A bull call spread usually has:
q4.explain: Long a low-strike call and short a high-strike call, both risk and reward are capped.

q5.prompt: The main risk of a short straddle is:
q5.o1: A large one-sided move causes expanding losses
q5.o2: Only the premium is at risk
q5.explain: Short calls and puts can both lose heavily if the underlying makes a large move.

q6.explain: Nonlinear books need joint shocks and liquidity assumptions.

q1.prompt: What discount rate is most commonly used in a DCF?
q1.o1: Risk-free rate
q1.o2: Loan rate
q1.explain: WACC reflects the cost of equity and debt capital.

q2.prompt: How is terminal value usually estimated?
q2.o2: Gordon growth model or exit multiple
q2.explain: Terminal value commonly uses perpetual growth or an exit multiple.

q3.prompt: What is the core of relative valuation?
q3.o1: Price the target using peer multiples
q3.explain: Relative valuation places the target in a comparable-company framework.

q4.prompt: A first-day IPO premium usually means:
q4.o1: The offer price is above the first-day close
q4.o2: The first-day close equals the offer price
q4.o4: The first-day close is above the offer price
q4.explain: First-day premiums are common when demand is strong or pricing is conservative.

q5.prompt: A deal described as EPS-accretive means:
q5.explain: Accretion means EPS rises, but it does not necessarily create economic value.

q6.prompt: What should an acquirer focus on?
q6.explain: Price, financing, synergies and integration all affect deal success.

q1.prompt: A central-bank rate cut usually has what effect on bond prices?
q1.o1: Bond prices fall
q1.o2: Bond prices rise
q1.explain: Lower rates make existing fixed coupons more attractive, so prices rise.

q2.prompt: An inverted yield curve means:
q2.o1: Short-term yields are above long-term yields
q2.o2: Long-term yields are above short-term yields
q2.o3: All maturities have the same yield
q2.explain: Inversion is often read as a slowdown or recession signal.

q3.prompt: The approximate real yield is:
q3.explain: Real yield measures purchasing-power return after inflation.

q4.prompt: The core risk of a carry trade is:
q4.o4: A high-yield currency suddenly depreciates or the rate differential narrows
q4.explain: Carry has limited upside, but FX and risk-appetite reversals can cause large losses.

q5.explain: Longer duration means a larger price response to yield changes.

q6.prompt: A macro regime framework usually tracks:
q6.explain: Growth, inflation, policy and liquidity together define the regime.

q1.prompt: The bid-ask spread is essentially:
q1.o1: The cost of immediate execution
q1.o2: A company dividend
q1.explain: The spread is the price of liquidity.

q2.prompt: Market-maker risks include:
q2.explain: Market makers hold inventory and can be picked off by informed traders.

q3.prompt: Price impact of a large order usually:
q3.explain: Larger and faster orders consume more depth.

q4.prompt: A VWAP algorithm usually aims to:
q4.explain: VWAP slices orders according to the volume profile.

q5.o1: Market makers are picked off by informed traders, eroding spread income
q5.explain: Information asymmetry makes market makers bear unfavorable fills.

q6.prompt: Market quality can be measured by:
q6.o4: The number of letters in the ticker
q6.explain: Liquidity, cost and stability together determine market quality.

glossary.title: Financial Glossary
glossary.subtitle: Understand terms in Chinese and English. {count} foundational concepts included.
glossary.twoLanguages: Every term includes explanations in both languages
glossary.disclaimer: Definitions are simplified for teaching and are not investment advice.

stock.name: Stock
stock.def: A tradable certificate representing a share of ownership in a company. Holding stock makes you a shareholder with a proportional claim on profits and residual assets.
stock.example: A company issues one million shares. Owning 1,000 shares gives you 0.1% ownership.

shareholder.name: Shareholder
shareholder.def: A person or institution that owns shares in a company. Shareholders typically have voting rights, dividend rights and the right to transfer their shares.
shareholder.example: When you buy AURA, you become one of Auralis Robotics' shareholders.

ticker.name: Ticker symbol
ticker.def: A short code used by an exchange to identify a listed company, usually one to five letters.
ticker.example: AURA is the ticker for Auralis Robotics in this game.

marketCap.name: Market capitalisation
marketCap.def: The total market value of a company, equal to share price times shares outstanding. It reflects overall company size, not the price of one share.
marketCap.example: $42.50 × 180 million shares = about $7.65 billion market cap.

sharePrice.name: Share price
sharePrice.def: The current market price of one share, continually updated by quotes and trades.
sharePrice.example: A last price of $42.50 means the most recent trade happened at that price.

exchange.name: Stock exchange
exchange.def: An organised marketplace that matches buy and sell orders, publishes prices and sets trading rules. The exchange itself does not trade shares.
exchange.example: All fictional company orders in this game match on the simulated exchange.

broker.name: Broker
broker.def: A financial firm or platform that accepts investor orders and sends them to an exchange for execution. Brokers charge commissions.
broker.example: The order ticket in this game plays the role of a broker.

bid.name: Bid
bid.def: The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay. Sells usually execute at the bid.
bid.example: A bid of $49.98 means someone is willing to buy at that price.

ask.name: Ask
ask.def: The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept. Buys usually execute at the ask.
ask.example: An ask of $50.02 means someone is willing to sell at that price.

spread.name: Bid/ask spread
spread.def: The difference between the ask and the bid. It is an implicit trading cost and is usually wider for less liquid stocks.
spread.example: Bid $49.98 and ask $50.02 means a $0.04 spread.

marketOrder.name: Market order
marketOrder.def: An order to trade immediately at the best available price. It prioritises execution speed over price certainty.
marketOrder.example: A market buy of 10 shares fills at the current ask.

limitOrder.name: Limit order
limitOrder.def: An order that sets a maximum purchase price or minimum sale price. It fills only at that price or better.
limitOrder.example: With the market at $50, a buy limit at $48 fills only if the price falls to $48 or lower.

costBasis.name: Cost basis
costBasis.def: The total amount paid for a position, including the purchase price and buy fees. Average cost = cost basis ÷ shares held.
costBasis.example: Buying 20 shares at $50 with a $1 commission gives a $1,001 cost basis.

unrealizedPnl.name: Unrealized P&L
unrealizedPnl.def: The floating gain or loss on a position you still hold, equal to current market value minus cost basis. It moves with the price.
unrealizedPnl.example: Cost basis $1,001, current value $1,100: unrealized gain of $99.

realizedPnl.name: Realized P&L
realizedPnl.def: The gain or loss locked in after selling, equal to net sale proceeds minus the matching cost basis.
realizedPnl.example: Net sale proceeds $1,099 against a $1,001 cost basis: realized gain of $98.

returnRate.name: Return
returnRate.def: P&L expressed as a percentage of the capital invested, allowing comparison across different position sizes.
returnRate.example: Invest $1,001 and gain $98: a return of about 9.79%.

commission.name: Commission
commission.def: A fee charged by a broker for executing a trade. Commissions directly reduce net profit.
commission.example: This game charges a flat $1.00 commission per fill.

liquidity.name: Liquidity
liquidity.def: How easily a stock trades and how close fills are to the expected price. Liquid stocks have tight spreads and fast execution.
liquidity.example: A heavily traded large cap is usually more liquid than an obscure small cap.

slippage.name: Slippage
slippage.def: The difference between the expected price at order entry and the actual fill. It is more visible in volatile or illiquid markets.
slippage.example: You see $50.00 but fill at $50.40; the extra $0.40 is slippage.

dividend.name: Dividend
dividend.def: Cash a company distributes to shareholders from profits. It is not guaranteed: the payout can be cut, suspended or cancelled.
dividend.example: You hold 100 shares with a $0.60 dividend per share, so you receive $60 in cash.

dividendYield.name: Dividend yield
dividendYield.def: Annual dividend per share ÷ current share price × 100%. A falling price raises the yield, but that does not make the company stronger.
dividendYield.example: Annual dividend $1.20 per share and a $40.00 price give a yield of 3.00%.

exDividendDate.name: Ex-dividend date
exDividendDate.def: Buyers on or after this date normally do not receive the declared dividend, and the share price adjusts down by roughly the dividend.
exDividendDate.example: Hold 200 shares paying $0.50 each before the ex-date to receive $100; the price moves from about $25.00 to $24.50.

payoutRatio.name: Payout ratio
payoutRatio.def: Dividend per share ÷ earnings per share. It shows how much profit is distributed rather than retained for reinvestment.
payoutRatio.example: EPS of $2.00 with a $1.00 annual dividend gives a 50% payout ratio.

growthStock.name: Growth stock
growthStock.def: A company growing revenue and earnings faster than the market, usually reinvesting profits, paying little or no dividend, with higher valuation and volatility.
growthStock.example: A company growing revenue 25% a year may earn a high P/E, but the price can fall sharply when growth slows.

valueStock.name: Value stock
valueStock.def: A stock priced low relative to earnings, assets or cash flow. It may be undervalued, or cheap because fundamentals are weakening.
valueStock.example: A P/E of 10 may look cheap, but you still need to check whether earnings are stable.

cyclicalStock.name: Cyclical stock
cyclicalStock.def: A stock whose earnings swing with the economic cycle, common in industrials, materials, energy and discretionary consumer sectors.
cyclicalStock.example: Orders and profits rise in expansions and can fall sharply in recessions.

etf.name: ETF
etf.def: A basket of assets traded on an exchange like a stock, usually tracking an index, sector or theme.
etf.example: One broad-market ETF share gives exposure to all of its underlying holdings.

diversification.name: Diversification
diversification.def: Spreading money across different assets to reduce company- or sector-specific risk. It cannot remove overall market risk.
diversification.example: Spreading money equally across three sectors softens the impact of one company failing.

compounding.name: Compounding
compounding.def: Reinvesting interest or returns so that future periods earn a return on them too. The effect grows with time.
compounding.example: $1,000 at 8% compounded annually is about $2,158.92 after 10 years.

candle.name: Candlestick
candle.def: A chart shape built from one period's open, high, low and close; the body connects open and close while wicks reach the high and low.
candle.example: Open $48, high $52, low $46.5, close $51.2 forms a bullish candle.

sma.name: Simple moving average (SMA)
sma.def: The arithmetic average of the last N closes, used to smooth noise and observe trend.

rsi.name: Relative Strength Index (RSI)
rsi.def: A momentum indicator comparing recent gains and losses on a 0–100 scale, with common thresholds of 70 and 30.
rsi.example: RSI above 70 shows strong momentum and possible overbought conditions, but does not guarantee a fall.

incomeStatement.name: Income statement
incomeStatement.def: A report starting with revenue, subtracting costs and expenses and ending with net income; margins measure profitability.
incomeStatement.example: Revenue $1,000M, gross profit $520M and net income $200M gives a 20% net margin.

balanceSheet.name: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.def: A snapshot of assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity; the identity is assets = liabilities + equity.

freeCashFlow.name: Free cash flow
freeCashFlow.def: Operating cash flow minus capital expenditure; cash available for dividends, buybacks and debt repayment.
freeCashFlow.example: Operating cash flow $300M minus capex $80M gives free cash flow of $220M.

dcf.name: Discounted cash flow (DCF)
dcf.def: Valuation that discounts future free cash flow at a risk-adjusted rate and adds a terminal value to estimate enterprise value.
dcf.example: Next-year FCF of $100M at a 10% discount rate is worth about $90.91M today.

gdp.name: Gross domestic product (GDP)
gdp.def: The total output of an economy over a period, used to measure economic growth.
gdp.example: GDP growing 3% year over year usually means an expanding economy.

inflation.name: Inflation
inflation.def: A broad and sustained rise in prices, which reduces the purchasing power of cash and fixed income.
inflation.example: At 4% inflation, goods costing 100 today may cost about 104 next year.

interestRate.name: Interest rate
interestRate.def: The cost of money. Higher rates raise discount rates and funding costs, usually lowering asset valuations.
interestRate.example: A discount rate rising from 8% to 10% lowers the present value of future cash flow.

assetAllocation.name: Asset allocation
assetAllocation.def: The process of dividing money across asset classes and weights, shaping a portfolio's risk and return.
assetAllocation.example: A 60% stock / 40% bond portfolio is usually steadier than an all-stock portfolio.

positionSizing.name: Position sizing
positionSizing.def: Calculating position size from acceptable risk and stop distance rather than buying on impulse.
positionSizing.example: A $10,000 account risking 1% with $4 risk per share buys 25 shares.

drawdown.name: Drawdown
drawdown.def: The fall in equity from a previous peak; large drawdowns significantly slow compounding.
drawdown.example: Falling from $10,000 to $6,000 is a 40% drawdown.

momentum.name: Momentum
momentum.def: The tendency of recent price trends to persist; momentum strategies buy strength and sell weakness.
momentum.example: A stock that outperformed over three months may stay in a momentum portfolio.

shortSelling.name: Short selling
shortSelling.def: Borrowing shares to sell them now, aiming to buy them back cheaper and profit from the difference.
shortSelling.example: Short at $50 and cover at $40 for a $10 per-share gross profit.

margin.name: Margin
margin.def: The equity that must be posted to cover potential losses on borrowed cash or securities.
margin.example: Buy $15,000 of stock with $10,000 of your own cash; the margin ratio is 2/3.

marginCall.name: Margin call
marginCall.def: A broker demand to add funds or face forced liquidation when equity falls below maintenance.
marginCall.example: A price drop pushes equity below maintenance and the account is liquidated.

stopOrder.name: Stop order
stopOrder.def: An order that becomes a market order once the trigger price is reached, used to cap losses.
stopOrder.example: Buy at $100 with a $92 sell stop; a break below sells at market.

trailingStop.name: Trailing stop
trailingStop.def: A stop that tightens as the price moves favourably and never loosens.
trailingStop.example: Buy at $100 with a $6 trail; after $120 the stop moves to $114.

orderBook.name: Order book
orderBook.def: The list of resting bids and asks by price, showing size at each level.
orderBook.example: Bid $49.99 and ask $50.01 give a $0.02 spread.

optionContract.name: Option contract
optionContract.def: Gives the buyer the right to buy or sell the underlying at the strike on expiry, in exchange for a premium.
optionContract.example: An AURA $55 call with 30 days left costs $1.20.

callOption.name: Call option
callOption.def: The right to buy the underlying at the strike on expiry; a bullish expression.
callOption.example: A $50 call has $10 of intrinsic value when the stock reaches $60.

putOption.name: Put option
putOption.def: The right to sell the underlying at the strike on expiry; used for bearish views or hedging.
putOption.example: A $50 put has $10 of intrinsic value when the stock falls to $40.

strikePrice.name: Strike price
strikePrice.def: The contracted price at which the underlying can be bought or sold; it sets intrinsic value.
strikePrice.example: A $50 call with spot at $55 has $5 of intrinsic value.

optionPremium.name: Option premium
optionPremium.def: The price paid for the option, equal to intrinsic value plus time value.
optionPremium.example: $2 intrinsic plus $1.10 time value gives a $3.10 premium.

impliedVolatility.name: Implied volatility
impliedVolatility.def: The market’s price for future movement; higher implied volatility makes options more expensive.
impliedVolatility.example: When implied volatility rises from 30% to 40%, call and put premiums usually rise.

greeks.name: Greeks
greeks.def: Sensitivities of option prices to different inputs: Delta, Gamma, Theta, Vega and Rho.
greeks.example: A delta of 0.5 means the premium rises about $0.50 for a $1 move.

assignment.name: Assignment
assignment.def: When an in-the-money option expires, the seller is obligated to perform under the contract.
assignment.example: A short $50 call with the stock at $60 must deliver at $50 or cash-settle.

coveredCall.name: Covered call
coveredCall.def: Holding 100 shares and selling one call; the stock covers delivery in exchange for premium.
coveredCall.example: Hold $50 stock and sell a $55 call for $1.50.

cashSecuredPut.name: Cash-secured put
cashSecuredPut.def: Selling a put while reserving strike × 100 in cash, accepting a possible purchase at the strike.
cashSecuredPut.example: Sell a $45 put for $1.20 and reserve $4,500.

verticalSpread.name: Vertical spread
verticalSpread.def: A long and a short option with the same expiry and different strikes, expressing direction with defined risk.
verticalSpread.example: Buy the $50 call and sell the $55 call for a $2 net debit.

straddle.name: Straddle
straddle.def: Buying a call and a put at the same strike and expiry; a bet on large movement rather than direction.
straddle.example: A $50 straddle costs $400 with breakevens at $46 and $54.

strangle.name: Strangle
strangle.def: Buying out-of-the-money calls and puts at different strikes for less premium but needing a larger move.
strangle.example: A $55 call and $45 put cost $200 with breakevens at $44 and $56.

futuresContract.name: Futures contract
futuresContract.def: An agreement to trade the underlying at a fixed price on a future date, requiring margin and P&L on full notional.
futuresContract.example: One $50 future has $5,000 notional and about $750 margin.

basis.name: Basis
basis.def: The futures price minus spot, usually reflecting carry and converging toward expiry.
basis.example: Spot $50 and futures $50.33 give a $0.33 basis.

hedge.name: Hedge
hedge.def: An offsetting position that lowers directional risk but leaves basis, correlation and margin risk.
hedge.example: Hold $50,000 of stock and short an equivalent futures notional.

systemicRisk.name: Systemic risk
systemicRisk.def: Risk that spreads through leverage, liquidity and counterparty chains across the market.
systemicRisk.example: Forced selling pushes prices down and triggers more liquidation and liquidity stress.

nav.name: Net asset value (NAV)
nav.def: Fund assets minus liabilities divided by fund shares, showing what one fund share is worth.
nav.example: Assets 120m, liabilities 10m and 10m shares give NAV = 11.

riskBudget.name: Risk budget
riskBudget.def: A method that allocates total portfolio risk across assets or strategies, focusing on risk contribution rather than capital weight alone.
riskBudget.example: Two strategies each hold 50% of capital but one contributes 80% of volatility; risk budgeting cuts its weight.

attribution.name: Performance attribution
attribution.def: An analysis that decomposes portfolio return into allocation, selection, interaction and fee sources.
attribution.example: The portfolio beats its benchmark by 2%, with 1.2% attributed to a technology overweight.

sharpeRatio.name: Sharpe ratio
sharpeRatio.def: Excess return divided by volatility, measuring reward per unit of risk.
sharpeRatio.example: With 12% return, 3% risk-free rate and 18% volatility, Sharpe = 0.5.

lookAheadBias.name: Look-ahead bias
lookAheadBias.def: Using information that was not available at the time in a backtest, inflating results.
lookAheadBias.example: Generating today’s signal from the next 20 days of returns cannot be traded live.

factorModel.name: Factor model
factorModel.def: A model that explains asset returns with common factors such as market, industry and style.
factorModel.example: A portfolio with 0.8 value exposure benefits when value rebounds.

overfitting.name: Overfitting
overfitting.def: A model fits noise in the training data and performs much worse out of sample.
overfitting.example: A 90% training accuracy and 52% out-of-sample accuracy means the model memorised noise.

volatilitySmile.name: Volatility smile
volatilitySmile.def: Implied volatility differs by strike, often forming a smile or skew.
volatilitySmile.example: Low-strike puts show higher IV than at-the-money options, producing a downward slope.

deltaHedge.name: Delta hedging
deltaHedge.def: Using the underlying to offset an option book’s Delta exposure, making it temporarily neutral to small price moves.
deltaHedge.example: A book with 500 shares of Delta is temporarily neutral after shorting 500 shares.

gammaScalping.name: Gamma scalping
gammaScalping.def: Buying options and dynamically delta hedging to profit when realised volatility exceeds implied volatility.
gammaScalping.example: When realised volatility exceeds IV, repeated hedge adjustments can cover the option cost.

wacc.name: WACC
wacc.def: The weighted average cost of equity and debt capital, commonly used as the DCF discount rate.
wacc.example: With 12% equity cost, 5% debt cost and 50/50 weights, after-tax WACC is about 8.5%.

comps.name: Comparable company analysis
comps.def: Pricing a target using valuation multiples from similar companies.
comps.example: A peer average P/E of 18 and target EPS of 2 imply about 36 per share.

dilution.name: Dilution
dilution.def: Issuing new shares reduces existing shareholders’ ownership percentage.
dilution.example: A 20% share issuance dilutes existing owners’ stakes.

ipo.name: Initial public offering (IPO)
ipo.def: A company’s first public share sale and listing.
ipo.example: Priced at 30 and closing at 36 on day one is a 20% first-day premium.

yieldCurve.name: Yield curve
yieldCurve.def: The relationship between government bond yields across maturities.
yieldCurve.example: Two-year 4.5% and ten-year 3.8% is an inverted curve.

carryTrade.name: Carry trade
carryTrade.def: Borrowing in a low-yield currency and investing in a high-yield currency to earn the rate differential.
carryTrade.example: Borrowing at 1% to invest at 5% implies 4% carry, but currency depreciation can wipe it out.

marketMaker.name: Market maker
marketMaker.def: A firm that continuously quotes bid and ask prices to provide liquidity.
marketMaker.example: After buying 10,000 shares, a long-inventory maker lowers the bid to encourage selling.

priceImpact.name: Price impact
priceImpact.def: A large order consumes order-book depth and moves the price.
priceImpact.example: Buying more than the best-level depth worsens the average fill.

adverseSelection.name: Adverse selection
adverseSelection.def: Information asymmetry makes market makers more likely to trade with informed counterparties.
adverseSelection.example: The price rises right after a maker buys, eroding spread income.

buy.market: A market buy fills immediately at the ask and makes you a shareholder.
buy.limit: A limit buy waits for the price to reach your limit or lower.
buy.stop: A buy stop becomes a market buy when the price rises to the trigger.
buy.trailing: A trailing buy stop moves its trigger down as the price falls, protecting a short.
buy.stop-limit: A buy stop-limit triggers first, then buys only at or below your limit; it may not fill.
buy.oco: OCO is for selling or covering: take-profit and stop-loss rest together, and one leg cancels the other.

sell.market: A market sell fills immediately at the bid and locks in realised P&L.
sell.limit: A limit sell waits for the price to reach your limit or higher.
sell.stop: A sell stop becomes a market sell when the price falls through the trigger.
sell.trailing: A trailing sell stop ratchets up with the price to lock in part of the gain.
sell.stop-limit: After the trigger, a sell stop-limit only fills at or above your limit; it may not fill.
sell.oco: OCO rests a take-profit limit sell and a stop-loss sell; whichever fills first cancels the other.

short.market: A market short borrows and sells now; proceeds count as collateral.
short.limit: A limit short waits for the price to rise to your limit before selling.
short.stop: A short stop covers at market if the price rises to the trigger.
short.trailing: A trailing short stop moves its trigger down as the price falls.
short.stop-limit: A short stop-limit only sells at or better than the limit after its trigger.
short.oco: OCO does not open shorts; it protects an existing position.

cover.market: A market cover buys back the borrowed shares immediately and locks in realised P&L.
cover.limit: A limit cover waits for the price to fall to your limit before buying.
cover.stop: A cover stop buys back at market if the price rises to the trigger.
cover.trailing: A trailing cover stop moves its trigger down as the price falls.
cover.stop-limit: A cover stop-limit buys back only at or below the limit after the trigger.
cover.oco: OCO can rest a cover take-profit limit and a cover stop; the first fill cancels the other.

p7.i1: Eight career ranks with verified promotion requirements and scheduled salary
p7.i2: Fund setup with strategy templates, risk profiles and three AUM tiers
p7.i3: Client subscriptions and redemptions, management fees and high-water-mark performance fees
p7.i4: Staff roles, position and cash limits, closure conditions and a peer fund leaderboard

p8.title: Phase 8 · Quant Lab
p8.text: Run independent strategy backtests on completed daily bars and rank the market by historical factors.
p8.i1: Five presets: buy-and-hold, moving-average cross, RSI mean reversion, momentum and range breakout
p8.i2: Signals confirm at the close and fill at the next open; grid optimisation checks overfitting out of sample
p8.i3: Total and annualised return, max drawdown, Sharpe, win rate, exposure and a trade log
p8.i4: Momentum, low-volatility, trend, valuation and news-sentiment factors, plus logistic and small neural-network selection

p9.title: Phase 9 · Multi-asset & automation
p9.text: Extend macro, fund and quant tools into more asset classes and scheduled execution.
p9.i1: Commodities (gold / silver / oil / copper / natural gas) and crypto (BTC / ETH / SOL) with fractional units and daily marking
p9.i2: Fund auto rebalancing: execute the strategy plan at day close on a schedule while keeping manual execution and risk checks
p9.i3: Calendar event shocks: CPI / payrolls / GDP / PMI / central-bank surprises transmit to simulated prices by beta
p9.i4: Automatic ML hyperparameter search plus news-sentiment-change and volume-attention factors

p10.title: Phase 10 · Strategy research and deeper models
p10.text: Push fund plans and quant research into verifiable parameter selection, factor premia and deeper models.
p10.i1: Fund sizing research: a 100-set holdings / cash / interval grid, in-sample selection, out-of-sample validation and one-click apply
p10.i2: Multi-factor regression: pooled cross-sectional OLS, factor premia, Rank IC and R²
p10.i3: Two-hidden-layer networks with their own auto-tuning, in-sample validation and feature importance
p10.i4: Money-flow factor: volume accumulated by price direction to measure net buying pressure

p11.title: Phase 11 · Intraday data, optimisation and fine attribution
p11.text: Add intraday observation, executable weight optimisation and finer holding attribution, plus an optional external live-quote channel.
p11.i1: Record an intraday candle per tick and switch the trading chart between daily and intraday
p11.i2: Optional external JSON quote feed with URL / interval settings, reference quotes and source time on the Market page, isolated from the simulated account
p11.i3: Portfolio optimiser with constrained minimum variance, inverse-volatility risk parity and mean-variance, producing a weight-based rebalance plan
p11.i4: Holding contribution plus Beta / momentum / volatility / P/E exposure, analyst-revision factors and intraday money flow

p12.title: Phase 12 · Multi-factor risk and transaction costs
p12.text: Extend portfolio optimisation with risk decomposition, stress testing and execution costs closer to reality.
p12.i1: Multi-factor risk model with market beta, size, value, momentum and low-volatility exposures
p12.i2: Factor / specific risk contribution split plus market-down, momentum-reversal, value-weakness and low-vol-weakness stress paths
p12.i3: Transaction-cost model: commission, bid/ask spread and volume-based market impact
p12.i4: Plan cost summary, cost-aware order sizing and execution slippage; taxes still follow external rules

p13.title: Phase 13 · Simplified tax profiles
p13.text: Add an optional teaching tax layer so fund net cash, plan costs and after-tax results are more complete.
p13.i1: Three simplified profiles: no tax, 15% capital gains, 25% capital gains plus a 0.1% transaction levy
p13.i2: Buy levies enter the cost basis; sell levies and capital gains tax reduce net cash
p13.i3: Account-level taxes paid plus the fund tax profile and cumulative taxes on the operations card
p13.i4: Plan costs include levies and capital gains tax; real regional rules and filing remain external

p14.title: Phase 14 · UK tax lab
p14.text: Add a 2026/27 UK tax estimate that shows the teaching tax cost of share trades, dividends and ISAs separately.
p14.i1: CGT: £3,000 annual exempt amount, 18% / 24% bands, same-day / 30-day / Section 104 matching
p14.i2: Dividend tax: £500 allowance and 10.75% / 35.75% / 39.35% rate bands
p14.i3: ISA exemption and £20,000 allowance; 0.5% SDRT on UK share purchases and a fixed teaching FX rate
p14.i4: Tax Lab page, disposal and dividend detail, warnings, source links and bilingual tests; educational estimate only

2008.title: 2008 Financial Crisis
2008.subtitle: Lehman, bailouts and the bottom
2008.desc: Start on the eve of the crisis and live through the subprime shock, Lehman's collapse, TARP and the 2009 bottom using real Nasdaq daily bars.
2008.tip1: Leverage and liquidity contract together in a crisis, so drawdowns dwarf normal volatility.
2008.tip2: Correlations rise in a crisis, so diversification can temporarily fail.
2008.tip3: Policy pivots often precede the bottom, but nobody can pick it precisely.

2015.title: 2015–2026 Long Cycle
2015.subtitle: Low rates, pandemic, hikes and AI
2015.desc: Replay real US stocks from 2015 onward across technology, healthcare, industrials, energy, utilities and communication: trade tensions, the pandemic crash, the hiking cycle and the AI wave.
2015.tip1: Long-term returns come from a few big trends, but the path includes drawdowns beyond 30%.
2015.tip2: Concentrated positions look brilliant in rallies and amplify losses in drawdowns.
2015.tip3: The replay only shows data up to today; do not replace decision-making with hindsight.

2020.title: 2020 Pandemic Crash & Rebound
2020.subtitle: Circuit breakers, zero rates and a tech bull market
2020.desc: Start at record highs, live through three circuit breakers, zero rates and a historic tech rebound, then the vaccine breakthrough.
2020.tip1: Crashes move fast; position sizing and a cash buffer matter more than calling the bottom.
2020.tip2: The policy bottom and the market bottom may differ; rebounds often precede economic recovery.
2020.tip3: Different sectors recovered at very different speeds in the same crisis.

2022.title: 2022 Rate-Hike Drawdown
2022.subtitle: Inflation, hikes and a growth de-rating
2022.desc: Replay real US stocks through a hiking cycle: growth valuation compression, bear-market rallies and the year-end low.
2022.tip1: Rising rates lower the value of distant cash flows; long-duration growth stocks suffer most.
2022.tip2: Bear-market rallies can be violent without a trend reversal.
2022.tip3: Use the replay to test stops and sizing rules, not just hindsight.
